Seeds and Grain Acts
I am not trying to downgrade the Bill which is in front of us today, but with the economic difficulties suffered in the constituency I represent and other farming constituencies across Canada, one cannot help but wonder if this is not just an act of presence on the part of the Minister to introduce every three or four weeks a token Bill which does not deal with the difficulties of the farming sector and with the vicious attacks perpetrated on that industry by the Minister of Finance in his disastrous Budget, which does not deal with the cut-backs in the economic statement of last November 8 and with the $50 million cuts proposed in the Deputy Prime Minister's so-called review-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: A slashing exercise.

-which is really, of course, a slashing exercise, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) so aptly put it. That is what is wrong. There has not been a meaningful effort on the part of the Government of Canada to deal with agriculture. Every now and then there is a token Bill presented on issues which may or may not be important. We see token Bills introduced which deal with housekeeping issues Bills or which were introduced by the previous Government and which died on the Order Paper. Those kinds of Bills are the ones we see introduced by the Government instead of providing the assistance which it chose to promise to the Canadian people last July and August.
I hope that in the response delivered by the Minister of Agriculture or more probably now by his Parliamentary Secretary, those issues will be addressed and that we will hear statements as to the farm debt crisis, the dairy policy and the drought aid for the West. What is going to happen with the fuel tax? Are there going to be rebates? Has the Minister made representations to the Minister of Finance on behalf of the farmers? Where are we with the red meat stabilization plan at this point in terms of negotiation with various groups? What about bankruptcy legislation and all the other issues with which we should be dealing? That is what 1 want as well as my colleagues in our Party, and I am sure all Hon. Members of this House want the Minister of Agriculture to address these issues with or without the introduction of the new Seeds Act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some trepidation in this debate because one of the main things this Bill does is to insert a word into an existing Bill. That word is "quality". So if we are going to have you, Mr. Speaker, interpret the happenings in this House as being out of order unless we are behaving in that manner, I will feel quite insecure about rising. But I have at least had the example of the two previous speakers and I do not feel quite so put upon at the moment because it appears that the order and method of carrying on debate in this House has changed very little as the result of the insertion of the word "quality" into the debate of the day.
That, I think, stresses very much what is happening with these amendments to the Seeds Act, Mr. Speaker. Who can object to the word "quality" being inserted into the Seeds Act?

September 12, 1985
Seeds and Grain Acts
We now have an Act respecting the testing, inspection, quality and sale of seeds. This is something which seed-growers have requested for some time. They have found themselves somewhat at a loss when looking at advertisements in the farm press or the general press to see seeds being advertised which do not meet the standards of the impression given in the advertisements. Advertisements for seeds which should not carry the designation "registered" have been appearing. No. 1 seed shows up quite regularly. This Act, as I interpret it, the last clause, at least, would require that advertisements of seeds which are not on the variety list would, have to be shown if they were given a designation, to be of the lowest quality for that particular kind of seed whether it be fescue seed or brome grass seed, wheat or whatever. So this does change in a very substantial way the method whereby seed is traded in the farming communities.
Whether the penalties and implementation being proposed here will make the new designations any more enforceable than were the old designations remains to be seen and I will come to that again a little later in my remarks because I have some concerns about the way we are apparently unable to regulate the laws which exist as they apply to seeds in this country. I am going to spend a few moments talking about the semi-dwarf wheat fiasco we went through late last winter and early spring. In the meantime, I would just like to continue with the evaluation and assessment of the words presented to us in this Bill which, other than what I have mentioned to this point, make very few changes.
There is a change to the penalties levied against those found guilty of an offence under the Act. Such offence must be prosecuted within two years of the alleged offence having taken place. In certain circumstances that could be extended to three years. A fairly major change is that the fines have been increased for offences under this Act. Formerly, the maximum fine was $500. That has now been increased to $25,000. The Minister is obviously attempting to bring the penalties up to date and I think this better reflects both the potential harm which can occur if the seed being sold is not what it is purported to be and the necessity for a deterrent for those who may have engaged in shady practices in the past. I suppose it is also in part a reflection of the inflation which has occurred since the last changes to the Seeds Act. I note, however, that the maximum jail penalty has not been changed, it is still two years. For clarification the Minister and the Government felt obliged to say that anyone not paying the fine does not automatically receive a jail sentence. So there have been some changes other than simply paying lip service to the fact that "quality" will now be part of the Act.
As well, there have been some slight changes to the definition of "sell". Previous to this Bill the Act gave only a short description of what selling seed was. That definition has been broadened to include "agree to sell or keep, transit, send, convey, deliver for sale or agree to exchange". All of those categories are now within the ambit of the Act and, hopefully,
will make possible better control over the advertising and marketing of seed products in this country.
The move to present the Canadian Seed Growers Association with some more responsibilities and powers is, I think, acceptable to most farmers. The exact extent of those powers and responsibilities is still not fully understood by all sides, but I think the committee is the place to investigate that further and I am prepared to pursue that when we get to committee.
There are some questions which have not been answered by these proposed amendments to the Act which I think are pertinent. I would have preferred that the Minister address these questions along with these amendments and I am sorry that he chose to introduce fairly limited amendments, thereby avoiding some of the larger issues surrounding the production and sale of seeds. In reinserting the issue of quality into the Act the Government is just bringing it up to date with what the seed growers have been trying to achieve over a number of years. They have always attempted to produce high quality seeds and maintain the highest possible standards for registration and grading. However, that raises some very pertinent questions given the cut-backs announced in the Budget last spring. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, cut-backs were announced in the area of the monitoring of seeds, establishing seed laboratories to test for germination and purity and to do quality control work. It seems a little ludicrous to insert the word "quality" into the system at the same time as the money which is used to maintain the system is being reduced. How are we going to maintain this quality that the Minister so proudly includes in the new title of his Act if the money and laboratories and personnel charged with maintaining that quality have been reduced? This question was not referred to by the Minister but I think he will have to give answers to the members of the committee when the Bill gets to that stage. How can grass seed producers in the Peace River area be certain of getting adequate tests on time if they have to rely on the private sector to build up gradually the expertise and equipment when they know that the process takes three or four years? How is the quality of a specific seed going to be maintained during a period of cut-backs when the procedures are not available quickly and consistently? It does not help a seed producer very much if he has to wait months for a purity or germination test. If he has a bunch of product waiting to be cleaned and there is some doubt about whether the germination or purity standards will be met, then he is going to be reluctant to go to the extra expense of cleaning it, bagging it and putting on the various tags and seals. Before they do that they have to clean a small sample and send it away to have these various tests done to see whether the binful from the field is of a quality that would warrant this being done. These kinds of questions have not been answered by the simple step of putting the word "quality" into the Act.
As well, I was a little unhappy that the Minister did not address the question of how we handle the unlicensed semidwarf wheats which are being grown in this country. They were never licensed to be grown here; they were imported illegally, on the surface at least. While the Minister had the
September 12, 1985

Act open I would have thought he would attempt to do away with the shortcomings in the law which have permitted the illegal importation of varieties which are not visibly different from the higher quality wheat that we grow in this country.
Canadian wheat is of the highest standard in the world. We make sales because of that reputation. We make sales to countries which are self-sufficient in wheat but need a stronger wheat to mix with their domestic varieties because theirs will not produce a good, consistent loaf of bread. Our reputation has kept Canadian wheat selling in world markets when the rest of the wheat-producing countries have found their granaries to be full before the new crop is harvested. Europe and the United States are sitting on huge surpluses, but we have been able to dispose of our wheat, in large part, because of the extremely good quality which we have maintained for that exportable product.
American plant breeders have not tried to produce these lower quality unlicensed semi-dwarf wheats in a way which will make them visibly different from our high quality bread wheats. Canadian plant breeders have a consistent and longstanding policy of ensuring that higher yielding but lower quality wheat is visibly different than higher quality wheats. We have licensed the semi-dwarf wheats which have higher yields than our hard red spring wheats which are of a higher quality, but one can see the difference because some of the kernels are of a lighter or white colour.
The Americans have been producing varieties that cannot be licensed in Canada because they are visually indistinguishable from our high quality wheat. Farmers have been bringing this wheat across our big undefended border. It is apparently very simple for them to bring it across. There is no provision in the Seed Act or in the Canada Grains Act to inspect or stop those grains which will be affected. Although the Minister has the Act open, he is not making any such proposals. Instead, the Minister of State for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) decided, almost on his own, but apparently with the approval of the Government, to change very effectively our whole quality system of wheat and grain production by sending a message to the farmers that it is okay to grow these unlicensed varieties. That is not acceptable in a parliamentary system. In the legal sense it is a very questionable process, but, what is more important for the farmers on the land, it puts our whole export potential in jeopardy.
About 80 per cent of the grains produced in western Canada are exported and a big portion of those grains consists of wheat. I pointed out earlier in my remarks that the sale of that wheat depends on the customer's understanding of the very high standard which we have. For the Minister to change those standards in a very derogatory was is a terrible thing for Canada's farmers. It is not maintaining the high quality that Canadian farmers expect and are used to. It denigrates the effort that we are trying to make through the Seeds Act to reintroduce quality.
Seeds and Grain Acts
The Minister should study this Act and consider ways to introduce quality into the export of wheat from this country. While preparing legislation which would include quality he should have kept the question of unlicensed semi-dwarf wheat in mind, addressed it in a realistic way, and presented proposals to the House of Commons so that the people of Canada would have a chance to comment on it. The Minister has abrogated his responsibilities. He has decided to work around the law and tell the farmers that it is all right to grow an unlicensed wheat which has never had the sanction of Canadian quality standards. You may think that this is a small thing and that it will all work out in the end, that the grain handling system will figure out a way to look after the problem, but how can it do so in a realistic way?
Consider the elevator agent who is the first in line receiving grain when it comes to market. A farmer can come in with a fine looking load of wheat and not say what variety it is. The elevator agent looks at it and says that it looks like a No. 1. The farmer has decided not to say anything even though he knows it is an unlicensed semi-dwarf wheat. Who can stop it? Chemical and baking tests will be made at the terminal elevator and that truckload may be caught there, but by that stage no one will know who delivered that grain. The elevator company which attempted to move it through the terminal system will be penalized because that grain will not be worth as much as was paid for it. They will have to find a market for that product now identified as being inferior. But what was there, in the initial stages, to keep that producer from accepting a higher price and higher grade on the understanding that it was high quality wheat? I submit there is nothing.
Given the current economic pressure that farmers are under-
Farmers are honest.
The Minister says that farmers are honest. 1 agree with that but that is the point I am getting to now.
You are saying that they are not.

I am saying that, given the economic pressure that farmers are under now, if they have the opportunity of getting an extra 60 cents a bushel by saying nothing, most of them are going to slough the honesty question aside and say nothing.
Are you saying we should remove the right for them to grow semi-dwarf?
I am saying that the Minister should be looking at-
If so, what would be the economic impact?

The economic impact that the Minister raises would not be very large. He has licence HY-320, which is virtually as good as the ones that you cannot distinguish. HY-320 has white wheats in it. You can tell visually that it is a lower quality wheat because of the colour constraints. The

September 12, 1985
Seeds and Grain Acts
market for those lower quality wheats can be met by HY-320. HY-320 does have a higher yield than the higher quality but higher priced regular wheats. There is no constraint in that case since HY-320 has been licensed, is legitimate and visibly distinguishable for farmers. However, to persist in permitting the illegal and unlicensed varieties which have never been sanctioned by the seed trade, the Department of Agriculture or the grains people in this country smacks of ineptitude. I believe the Government should have taken a much harder line on this issue and been much more honest with the farmers of the country with respect to the economic impact.
Many false figures were published last spring which indicated that there might be 20 per cent or 30 per cent of the wheats seeded to these particular unlicensed varieties. The Minister decided to be lenient with the farmers. The first figures that were released toward the end of the crop year and the beginning of the next crop year claimed that 20 per cent of farmers produced unlicensed wheats. However, when the figures were recalculated it was discovered that rather than 20 per cent, it was one-twentieth or 5 per cent rather than one-fifth. There was some expert juggling among some of those who supply information which I believe has created the kind of response given by the Minister.
I believe the ministries were misinformed as to the extent of the unlicensed varieties that were going to be seeded. I think they could have been much more firm and said that they do not sanction the seeding of these varieties because of the great impact not only this year but next year and the following year. Even if we tried to eliminate those varieties tomorrow, now that they have been expanded to such an extent in this crop year they will be coming through the system for years to come. They can be stored in granaries until they are no longer scrutinized. They can be blended with other higher quality grains which will make them very difficult to find. I believe we have left a bad mark on the reputation of Canada as a supplier of high quality wheat.
I admire the Minister for attempting to increase the quality standards of the Canada Seeds Act but I wish that, while he was trying to increase the quality of Canada seeds, he had addressed more directly and properly the problem of unlicensed semi-dwarf wheats that have been coming into this country illegally from the United States and elsewhere. It has become a blot against our reputation as a supplier of high quality red baking wheats in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity this morning to take part in the debate on this legislation and express my support for Bill C-64, which will soon be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture, where we hope to hear from the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who tends to rattle off what he has to say in two and a half minutes here in the House but is never around
to discuss the substance of a particular topic. Unfortunately, he is much too busy to attend committees of the House. That is too bad, because committees are often ideal for discussing legislation and making improvements, in this case, for the benefit of the Canadian public and the Canadian farm producers he is always referring to.
Mr. Speaker, in a number of ways this Bill is particularly significant for the seed industry here in Canada.

Pedigreed seed is the vehicle for transmitting the benefits of plant breeding research to the producer. That is why it is so important to guarantee that the farmer actually receives the product he assumes he is buying.

Under the present system in this country, it is very important, and has been for years, to safeguard the interests for the public and our producers.
The commercial seed industry, Mr. Speaker, generates $315 million in sales annually in this country alone, and forms the basis for Canada's grain industry, which exports surpluses with over $4 billion annually, while Canadian seed grain exports also represent some $50 million per year.

Without question, seeds are the single most important farm input. Without the proper seed planted at the right time, the impact of all other farm inputs-pesticides and fertilizers, for example-would be greatly diminished.
The last major changes to the Seeds Act were made in 1959 and a great deal has occurred in the seed growing industry since then. The legislation before us today has been in the works for several years, since 1977 as a matter of fact, and 1 commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) for taking the initiative to finally bring it forward. I think it is very important.
The Government of Canada has been involved in the regulation and control of seed varieties for the past 80 years. When our involvement began in 1905, the main objective was to control the sale of low vitality seeds, or seeds containing harmful weeds. In subsequent years, as the seed industry developped, the Act was amended to include a grading system for seed quality, a licensing system for crop varieties and labelling requirments that help the buyer to identify quality seeds.

Since major amendments were made to the Bill in 1959- [English]
-the seed growing industry has undergone a number of important changes. It has grown dramatically and, as the Minister pointed out in his remarks, there has been increasing involvement by the private sector in plant breeding and ownership.
One of the key elements of this Bill is that it will provide greater authority under the Seeds Act to protect against false
September 12, 1985

advertising and to strengthen the seed licensing system. This is an especially important initiative in view of the Minister's stated intention to bring forward plant breeders' rights legislation in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments to the Seeds Act being examined today will ensure that further privatization can proceed. In this way, there will be proper regulation and control of the quality and sale of seeds in this country. By making the-

Mr. Speaker, herring stocks have proved to be plentiful this fall in northwestern New Brunswick.
In fact the quota allowed by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) was caught within five days. Reaching the quota in so little time does show that herring stocks in the gulf are huge.
The fishing industry is now asking that the quota be raised so that fishing might continue. The industry has been unable to meet the market demand and is afraid of losing its foreign markets if it cannot fill its orders.
Given the high unemployment rate in the fishing communities of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, I urge the Minister to raise the quota immediately.
Undoubtedly the Minister is aware of the fact that this fish quota allocated to all New Brunswick fishermen has been caught only by fishermen from the northeast region.
Unfortunately the fishermen from the southeast region did not have an opportunity to take part in fishing because herring stocks had not yet reached the strait of Northumberland.
I would therefore urge the Minister to allocate a separate quota to fishermen of the southeast region so that, in the future, southeastern New Brunswick fishermen will be sure to take part in herring fishing.

RECOMMENDATION TO POSTPONE DATE FOR CLOSURE OF GULF REFINERY IN EAST MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to speak in my capacity as chairperson of the special committee established to make a study concerning the Eastern Montreal Gulf refinery located in my riding; this committee was struck by the Quebec caucus.
Considering the situation of the workers, Mr. Speaker, I would therefore ask the House and the Minister responsible to open discussions immediately with the owners of the Eastern Montreal Gulf refinery with a view to putting off any action and delaying the shutdown of the refinery until May 1986. Mr. Speaker, we hope that such a delay will enable prospective buyers to make their move and that our Government will find a solution.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians who watch television have been unable to avoid the slick ads appearing almost every day telling us what a great company CPR is, how it is involved in every aspect of Canadian life, how eager it is to serve the needs of the Canadian people, and how its employees are all part of one big family who just love to work for the C.P.R. Those ads would make hundreds of CPR employees laugh if recent decisions of the CPR were not having such adverse effects on them.
CPR has announced lay-offs in its Weston shops in Winnipeg, affecting some employees who have worked for the CPR for almost 30 years. Similarly thousands of CPR employees have been laid off from one end of Canada to the other in recent years.
CPR employees remember the promises made by the former Liberal Transport Minister who, along with the CPR and the CNR, assured the people of Canada that if only Parliament passed the legislation, which they brought forward wiping out the Crow rate agreement, thousands of new jobs would be provided.
In the same vein, when the new diesel shop was opened in Winnipeg by the CPR the former Minister assured people that 200 to 300 jobs would be created. Those of us who questioned the extravagant claims of the then Government and the rail-

September 12, 1985
ways were laughed at. Unfortunately, the concerns we expressed were only too true. In fact we were not tough enough in our criticisms.
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Once again, Mr. Speaker, I am bringing to the Government's attention the plight of the Canadian footwear industry which is desperately trying to stay in business in the face of unfair competition from off shore countries.
The Canadian footwear industry has been constant in its endeavours to secure a realistic limit on imports of footwear from other countries. It is not asking for the moon. It is not asking that imports be eliminated. What it is asking could not be more fair. It is that the Government limit imports to 50 per cent of the domestic market. The removal of footwear quotas would sound the death knell for the industry as well as cause the loss of 20,000 jobs.
Not only would the removal of the quotas result in lost jobs, but there would be the added burden on UIC and welfare, not to mention lost taxes at all levels of Government.
The extension of quotas on footwear imports for five years at 50 per cent of the Canadian market would create at least 6,000 new jobs, a positive shot in the arm for our economy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the Government to address itself to this problem in a positive way.

subtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT ONTARIO BE DECLARED BRUCELLOSIS FREE
RECOMMENDATION THAT ONTARIO BE DECLARED BRUCELLOSIS FREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this year, Quebec was declared brucellosis free. Although this is very good news and Quebec farmers are pleased, Ontario unfortunately was not so designated, which has created a major problem between Eastern Ontario and Quebec, especially in connection with the livestock trade.
In fact, today it is harder for a livestock trader in my riding to sell to Quebec than to the United States.
Since Ontario has had no cases of brucellosis for more than a year, I would urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to have Ontario declared brucellosis free immediately. Further delay will cause inconvenience and mean additional expenses for farmers and livestock traders in my riding and throughout Eastern Ontario.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF POLAR 8 ICEBREAKER-SUPPORT SOUGHT FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA SHIPYARDS
CONSTRUCTION OF POLAR 8 ICEBREAKER-SUPPORT SOUGHT FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA SHIPYARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Members applauded the announcement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on Tuesday asserting Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic and that part of this affirmation would be the construction of a Polar 8 icebreaker which could provide a continuous Canadian presence in our Arctic waters.
Today I would like to state the interests of British Columbia shipbuilders in the construction of this half a billion dollar vessel. As we well know, British Columbia shipyards, in their expertise and experience in the building of major icebrakers, are second in the world, second only to Finland, and have recently formed a consortium to bid, internationally, for building such icebreakers.
Let me say as well, and I am sure my Quebec colleagues, upon reflection, would have to agree, that if the construction of this icebreaker takes place in British Columbia, shared between North Vancouver and Victoria, substantial economic benefits will still accrue to central Canada, particularly to Quebec, which will supply much of the materials and components.
However, to construct the icebreaker in British Columbia would enable the West to share in these substantial benefits. So I urge my colleagues, given comparable costs, that in the interest of fairness for all Canadians, and to enable all parts of the country to benefit from this major project, they should to support a proposal from British Columbia shipbuilders to lead this project of such significance to Canada's sovereignty in the Arctic.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE-THREAT TO LUMBER EXPORTS
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE-THREAT TO LUMBER EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the forest industry in Canada faces a crisis as a result of the failure of the Mulroney Government to inform consumers and users of wood products in the United States properly about the implications of the Gibbons Bill now before the U.S. Congress.
This protectionist legislation, now supported by three-quarters of Congress, is likely to move forward in a matter of weeks. Within the Bill is a removal rights clause which will effectively change the rules of the game and allow the United States to place tariff walls and countervailing duties against our forest products.
Forestry is Canada's largest industry and largest source of balance of trade. One Canadian in ten relies on forestry for employment.
The Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) gutted Canada's strong position at a meeting with the Congressional
September 12, 1985

subcommittee on trade in Vancouver a month ago and has compounded this with further written criticism to Congress this week.
Surely with the United States moves on hogs and fish the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has awakened to the economic guillotine raised by the Gibbons Bill. I trust he will be making a statement in this House on actions he is taking to remedy the U.S. proposal and to prepare a survival plan for the 300 forest based communities that are at risk should the Gibbons Bill become law.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FOREST FIRE-FIGHTERS-EXTENSION OF COVERAGE
BRITISH COLUMBIA FOREST FIRE-FIGHTERS-EXTENSION OF COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the summer recess of the House, Kootenay West was hit very hard by forest fires. Other ridings were similarly affected, although not all as severely as mine. As a result of this long hot summer, over 10,000 people were temporarily employed by the Province of B.C. to combat these fires. They worked hard and long and, at times, in serious danger. However, they were the unfortunate victims of a provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act which denied UIC coverage to temporary provincial governemnt employees working in a disaster situation.
In the remarkably short period of less than 30 days, the Cabinet responded to my urgent request that the UIC Act be amended to provide UIC coverage to forest fire-fighters.
There are those critics who suggest that to provide this UIC coverage to fire-fighters is to invite arson by those who would seek to generate their own employment by starting a forest fire. To my knowledge there were only two cases of arson involved in all the hundreds of forest fires this summer in British Columbia. I have more faith in my fellow Canadians than to believe that the change in the Act invites arson. Therefore, at this time I should like to express my appreciation, and the appreciation of fire-fighters to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), the then Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty), and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser)-

subtopic: RECOMMENDATION TO INCREASE FUNDS FOR LOW-INCOME FAMILIES
RECOMMENDATION TO INCREASE FUNDS FOR LOW-INCOME FAMILIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian families are increasingly at a loss to understand the attitude of the Prime Minister and Conservative Members. Most of them wonder why families with children should give up $56 million in family assistance programs, when the Government has no trouble finding one billion to help people with deposits in excess of $60,000 in a bank that is in difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Conservative Members realize that low-income families,... even if the child tax credit is increased during this particular time and I am referring to the back-to-school season, most spouses need the family allowance cheque every month to buy school supplies and to pay for their children's recreation and extracurricular activities, so that children of poor families do not feel left out when they compare notes with children from families with average incomes.
Mr. Speaker, in the first year, that is 1986, the result of the Government's decision will be to reduce the family allowance by $22. Hon. Members here may think $22 is not much over one year, but most of these families need this money for their children.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore urge all Members of this House to ask the Prime Minister to establish a policy on the family, not by reducing spending on improving the quality of life but by increasing amounts available for improving the quality of life of families with children.

Mr. Speaker, among the many justifiable expectations the Canadian people have of their Members of Parliament is that we shall be competent, conscientious and courteous in the manner in which we conduct ourselves as their elected representatives. It is an unfortunate though largely unavoidable fact that many Canadians can only judge whether or not their expectations are being met by what they see during Question Period.
During this past spring and summer I received more negative comments concerning the conduct of Members during Question Period than on any other issue or topic. Indeed, the general consensus of opinion was that the cynical laughter, the pejorative mutterings, and the overt and often entirely irrelevant one-upmanship were more in keeping with immature school children still wrestling with their developing egos, than

September 12, 1985
with competent representatives consciously grappling with weighty matters of state.
It is of utmost importance that we remember who we are, where we are, and why we are here. Therefore I call upon all Hon. Members, myself included, to conduct ourselves in a manner becoming our privileges and responsibilities as Members of Parliament. I urge you, Mr. Speaker, to exercise the full weight of your authority to deal quickly and firmly with any Members violating the letter and spirit of the rules of the House, so that Canadians can be justifiably proud of their institution and their representatives.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE-LEVY ON HOG EXPORTS
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE-LEVY ON HOG EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years Canada and the United States have had virtual free trade in red meats. Imports by Canada of U.S. pork have at times amounted to between 14 per cent and 15 per cent of our pork consumption. While Canadian producers perceived the imports as reducing their price and market opportunities, they did not move to stop them even though subsidized corn was used in their production.
Now the situation is reversed and Canadian hog producers are stunned and confused by the signals being sent by the Americans who, when faced with less than 3 per cent of their market being filled by Canadian pork, moved quickly to file a countervail of 5.5 cents per pound against Canadian products. After spending several millions of dollars fighting the levy, Canadian pork producers succeeded in getting a partial lifting of the countervail on processed products, but it is still in effect on live hogs.
United States pork prices have not been changed by the levy. Canadian producers have suffered a general price decline of 5 cents or 6 cents per pound. If our two countries are serious about furthering free trade, then both countries must be involved in solving these trade disputes. Leaving that power with the International Trade Commission of the United States Department of Commerce does not provide any appearance of fair dealing on sensitive issues involving producers in the two countries. Such powers have to be shifted to a bilateral body if the current laudable efforts toward open and honest trade are to be continued. Failure to establish such an international body makes further free trade talks pointless until we can make the existing agreements work.

access to the United States market that we are considering these types of programs. We would hope that that kind of protectionism ceases to exist because we believe that fair trade and enhanced trade mean jobs for Canadians, and that is what we are committed to and trying to create.

On the
contrary, Mr. Speaker. We would assume that we would be able-as we have been able in the past-to eliminate these irritants, to the extent humanly possible, as they arise, as an indication of the kinds of ongoing and more durable relationships which can exist between our two countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the specific request of my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), I have decided to continue where I left off. I felt I could not leave any loose ends, especially since the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) is in the House. I am delighted with this unique opportunity to see the Hon. Member taking part and listening to the debate in the House. I shall nevertheless be brief, Mr. Speaker, since the time of the House is a precious commodity and we have already established some agreement on the Bill and its consequences.
Mr. Speaker, just before the House took recess this morning, I was saying that the new legislation will provide for more satisfactory regulation and control of the quality and sale of seeds in this country, by improving our system and making it more flexible. I think now we can say we have guarantees, as far as that is possible against the introduction of inferior varieties that are not adapted to our climate, and that for the years to come.
I want to proceed quickly with another important aspect, and I am referring to the increased penalties provided under the legislation. If we refer to page 4a of the Bill, we see that far more severe penalties are now provided under the proposed legislation and that persons who contravene its provisions will be severely punished. I feel this adds a guarantee of a certain degree of security to the present legislation.
I see that my comments command the sustained attention of the Opposition as usual, when we are talking about serious matters, Mr. Speaker. They must be having a hard time deciding who is going to be the new Opposition critic for agriculture. There seems to be a lot of enthusiasm for the job.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I would also like to comment on the work done by representatives of the Canadian Seed Growers Association whom I was able to meet several times and who must feel very uncomfortable when they hear what Opposition Members in the House have to say, because there is a vast difference between what they say and the interests of the Canadian associations. The sustained interest shown by this association over the past years has made it possible for the Government to introduce and improve legislation, with the

result that if the passage of this Bill is expedited, we shall have legislation that will be truly beneficial to our Canadian producers.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: How true! How true!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the debate on Bill C-64, an Act to amend the Seeds Act and the Canada Grain Act. Because this Bill was introduced on short notice, it was difficult to prepare for this debate and be briefed on the Bill. However, the Minister stated that this is a technical Bill which should be beneficial to groups involved in the production, marketing, distribution and maintenance of seeds. Of course, this is an important topic, especially in a highly developed and technologically advanced country like Canada. When this Bill goes to the legislative committee-the Hon. Member for Bellechasse (Mr. Blais) does not seem to realize that we have established a legislative committee to look after Bills in the future-I hope we will be able to study it in greater detail.
It appears from a quick review of the Bill that the Government, apart from clarifying definitions of such words as "to sell" and "grade", seems to have taken unto itself a great deal of power by regulation.
For instance, Clause 4 of the Bill gives the Governor in Council vast new powers relating to information, registration of seeds, and specifying terms and conditions under which seeds can be registered.
It also prescribes procedures for review of cases involving the refusal, suspension or cancellation of registration of seeds. In Clause 4(h.5) of the Bill it gives the Governor in Council the power by regulation in:
determining the cases in which and the conditions, including provision of a bond, under which seeds shall, for the purposes of this Act, be transported and stored on importation.
There is a great deal of concern in the agricultural community with the powers the Minister already has by regulation for the inspection of crops, especially with the decision made last November 8, a day which has become known in the agricultural community as black Thursday. The Government imposed an unprecedented $32 million worth of inspection charges on Canadian agriculture.
I have in my hand a letter from the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture denouncing those charges which have been imposed on agricultural production. These charges have come at a time when agricultural producers right across the nation are feeling disposessed by this Government. They are declaring bankruptcy and the incidents of foreclosure are in record numbers. In the first two months of this fiscal year, the Farm

September 12, 1985
Seeds and Grain Acts
Credit Corporation reported foreclosures were taking place 87 per cent more rapidly than last year, which works out to about 11 foreclosures a week.
Pressures are great on the producers and commodity prices are low. For instance, I am told the price of potatoes to the producers in Prince Edward Island and in New Brunswick are running at 2 cents a pound or a little over that while production costs are well above 4 cents a pound. How the Government can be imposing new inspection charges at this time is puzzling. These charges amount to 3 cents a pound-that is for the average 600 acre potato farm in Prince Edward Island-or $3,600 per farm. It is a massive increase for something which historically has been paid for by the Department of Agriculture on the understanding that the Government has a certain responsibility for quality, grading and inspection of crops in order to protect the quality, the sizing and the trade aspects of agricultural commodities.
The Government is claiming more regulatory powers in this Bill. We wonder whether this is just another phase of increasing these fees. In a letter, a copy of which was sent to me by the Secretary Manager of the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture, he speaks about inspection licence and fees regarding field crops. He points out that the new aspect to this issue is the requirement for a mandatory licensing for all shipments crossing provincial boundaries, for which a $500 annual licence fee will be required, and a 3 cent per hundredweight inspection fee. Prior to June, 1984, shippers of fresh products on a small scale individual farm basis have been exempt from licence fee which then was only $25. We see the licence fee going up from $25 to $500. No actual inspection of the product is conducted nor is it planned that such an inspection service should be provided. I inquired of the program officer in Moncton as to whether one licence by a commodity group or a maritime association such as like the Maritime Strawberry Council could accommodate the requirement of the regulation, and was told that it would not. Each individual shipper must be licensed whether selling his own product or someone else's product. I pointed out that this regulation effectively put small producers with sales of $ 1,000 a year out of business. Therefore, it would be in the best interests of Nova Scotia producers to protest the manner in which the inspection fees are being applied. A $500 annual licence fee for which no service is provided, thus effectively putting fresh dairy and vegetable producers out of business runs contrary to Nova Scotia federal agreements and a host of other goals for our crop community groups.
We can see that those fees which were imposed last fall, besides being unfair and unjust could hardly have been imposed at a worse time for so many commodity groups in Canada. They were just not imposed for horticultural products but only for meat inspection, hogs, beef and so on. It was done without very much concern for the current difficult time we are in. That $32 million in service charges was combined with drastic cuts in many other areas and was supplemented later in the Budget with another $50 million cut, about which everyone in the agricultural community is holding his breath because
people do not know where the other shoe will drop, whether there will be more service charges, a cut in the dairy subsidy, a cut in transportation or research. I hope the Minister when we get him before the committee will be able to clarify that point.
We do have new regulatory powers. We will want to know exactly how the Government plans to use those in the weeks ahead, if and when this legislation is passed by the committee and by the whole House. The Government seems to have imposed Draconian penalties under this Bill. The summary conviction penalty now of $500 for a minor infraction of the Seeds Act would seem to be adequate. That $500 penalty is to be increased to $25,000. I know we cannot ask questions in the House today at second reading as to why that amount is being increased, but surely a $25,000 fine is a very severe penalty for a minor infraction under this Act? As well, when a proceeding commences in a court on conviction on indictment, Clause 7 of the Bill reads:
(b) on conviction on indictment, to a fine in the discretion of the court or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years or to both.
A five year penalty for an infraction of this Act seems a very severe penalty. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister, whoever is carrying this Bill in the committee, will be able to explain why we would want to incarcerate somebody for five years for an infraction of the Seeds Act. I hope that that can be clarified for the members of the committee.
There is another aspect of the Bill about which I wonder whether it is in contravention of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Under Section 7 there are very broad powers regarding seizure. It seems to me that this Bill would give an inspector the right to seizure under Section 7. I am wondering whether that procedure can be exercised without the benefit of a search warrant. Surely an inspector cannot make seizures without the proper authority of a search warrant as is required by that section of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Yesterday we discussed in the House amendments which would do away with writs of assistance in drug legislation.
The concern of the House-and it is certainly that of Hon. Members on this side-is that although this Bill is probably necessary to improve the operation of the Seeds Act, why has the Government not come forward with substantive legislation? I am not aware of massive problems in the areas of licensing and the regulation of seeds. Obviously this legislation will enhance those processes. However, why has the Government not dealt with many other problems which are facing the Canadian agricultural community today? Why has there been no decision on drought assistance for the agricultural community in western Canada? The Hon. Member for Assiniboia, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson), has been thrashing around on this issue for two or three months. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said that he could not make a decision because that Parliamentary Secretary has been unable to make a report. Also he said that he hoped a report would be forthcoming in a few weeks.
September 12, 1985

I find it difficult to understand how the Government of Saskatchewan was able to make a decision in late July that it would pay a wintering benefit of some $60 per head of cattle, yet it took the Government of Canada and the committee it established another three or four weeks to decide to provide $30 per head for wintering and drought assistance. That announcement was made with a grand flourish and, lo and behold, we found that the Premier of Saskatchewan reached out and grabbed that $30 per head or $16 million and took it unto himself. The result is that farmers are no better off. It was a beautiful song and dance show. It was almost like the "sham on the rocks" in Quebec City. After the federal announcement, livestock producers ended up with the same $60 per head. As a matter of fact, they probably thought something would be forthcoming from the federal Government, but they ended up with nothing. The provincial Government effectively set the policy for assistance to the livestock industry back in late July. Why has it taken the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister so long to reach a decision about assistance or to make a recommendation to the Government in favour of assistance to grain producers?
I had an opportunity in late July to visit areas in southwestern Saskatchewan and to see the burnt crops. There will be no crop or very little crop this year. The Government brings in technical legislation when it should bring in substantive decisions and solutions. If it is beneficial, desirable and necessary for the Government to make known to livestock producers in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta how much will be available for this coming winter to keep their basic herds intact, surely it is equally valuable for grain producers. Although a seeds Bill is important and valuable, it seems to me that we should be talking about assistance to the wheat and grain growers of western Canada. In early August the wheat pool indicated that a program involving some $50 per acre or $500 million was needed. I had hoped the committee on the government side which is studying this matter sat down with the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other agricultural groups in Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Peace River country to get on with reaching a decision. When I asked the Minister about it in the House this week, he said that it would be another two or three weeks.
The situation is really desperate. Many of us have had a chance to visit those areas. We have seen the clips on television of farmers lining up at welfare offices looking for assistance. We have seen the statistics of the Farm Credit Corporation which indicate that in the first two or three months of this fiscal year that some 35 per cent or 40 per cent of foreclosures were on farm property. As a matter of fact, all foreclosures and bankruptcies are running at a rate of some 87 per cent or some 11 per week. Although we are glad to see this Bill before the House today, we would like to see substantive legislation and programs to rescue agricultural producers from the desperate situation in which they find themselves today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a couple of comments about some of the suggestions and accusations which were made by the Hon. Member, particularly those
Seeds and Grain Acts
relating to the drought. There is no question that the drought is a very serious situation and that it is very frustrating for farmers. It has gone on for a number of years in some of the serious drought areas and has involved a number of acres.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and that task force on drought have responded quickly. We felt that the main consideration had to be the livestock area. The Government supported the recommendations of the task force. We moved, and some $48 million is being paid right now-and many farmers have received their cheques-in terms of feed assistance for their herds. We felt that this was most important and we moved on phase one. The Hon. Member raised what we call phase two relating to crops and grain production. Surely he must understand that the crop reports have to come in. We are not only dealing with southern Saskatchewan. We are also dealing with Alberta, the Peace River and into British Columbia. I have recently checked with some Hon. Members from Alberta and they indicated that the crops in that area were less than 5 per cent harvested. It is impossible to get results from the crop insurance people. As well, in terms of what the Government has done, I am sure the Hon. Member is well aware that the federal Government does pay 50 per cent of the crop insurance premiums. In addition to that, last year the Government paid into the drought areas some $250 million. It is estimated that this year, the dollar value will probably go beyond $250 million. We have responded very positively. It is a downright shame that the Opposition has tried to capitalize on a very serious drought situation in order to make political headway. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they are not going to do this on the backs of western Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that he has responded. The Premier of Saskatchewan responded about two or three weeks before he did. The province essentially set the rate and the Government of Caanda simply offered half of the help. That is history now.
It is rather interesting that the Parliamentary Secretary has indicated that he made a report. If I heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) correctly yesterday, he said that he could not really make a decision because he was waiting for a report from the Parliamentary Secretary. It seems to me that they should get their stories straight so that they are both saying the same thing.
Dealing with the task force, the Parliamentary Secretary has said that it really cannot make a decision until all of the crop reports are in. There are many areas in western Canada where there are effectively no crops. I visited Assiniboia and southern Saskatchewan almost two months ago and there was no crop at that time. Things certainly have not improved since. As a matter of fact, getting the crop off is the problem. I believe we are talking about a question of confidence. We should ask if the Government is going to provide the assistance that is necessary.

September 12, 1985
Seeds and Grain Acts
In 1984 when the Liberal Party was in Government, there was a demand by all Members of the Tory Party who were sitting on this side of the House that the Government commit itself to crops that were destroyed in northeastern Saskatchewan. The Hon. Member who represents that area is in the House today. It was demanded that the Government make a commitment and the then Prime Minister, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), did make a commitment of $20 per acre. The Tories only paid half of that when they came into power.
For opposition Members to be asking when the Government is going to make a commitment to western agriculture at a time when the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has been demanding a commitment for the last three or four weeks is certainly not too soon. I am disappointed that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson), who obviously wields a great deal of power not only in his caucus but in the councils of the Government, was not able to say that the Government will make a decision within a week. If the Parliamentary Secretary makes a further comment today, I hope he will be able to make a commitment as to when the Government will help the grain producers of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to have you in the chair today to listen to a very important debate on agriculture. I am sure this debate is of grave importance to members of your constituency. Many of us in the West raise bird seed and I am sure many of your constituents, Mr. Speaker, feed canaries, budgies and so forth. I am pleased that you are here to listen to this debate.
Obviously the Member who just spoke was caught without his notes on the Seeds Act so he quickly grabbed some notes on the drought and decided to make a little speech on drought assistance. His argument dealt with who responded first. That is a typical Liberal argument. Liberal Members are not really sure what to do. There is no point in consulting so they just respond first and take credit for action on behalf of farmers. It does not really matter if they help the farmers or not. It is only important for them to get a press release out. That is the way the former Minister of Agriculture acted so often, unlike this Minister who has acted through legislation. Members of Parliament were busy last year and are already busy again dealing with issues that are important to agriculture.
During the previous Government, we often waited patiently for Mr. Whelan to come forward with legislation. The only times we debated agriculture were when we had an Opposition Day and opposition Members raised issues that were important to agriculture.
The question of who responded first is not important in my mind. The Parliamentary Secretary has done an excellent job on behalf of western farmers in being on the scene. He has discussed with them the difficulties that they face and has asked the farmers and organizations about the best possible way to respond to this year's drought. As he adequately explained, there was a need to act quickly as far as livestock producers were concerned because green feed had to be cut and farmers had to know whether or not they could afford to
purchase green feed for their livestock this year. That action has been taken and $48 million has been allocated by the federal Government. As well, monies have been allocated by the provincial Governments to respond to this very serious drought situation.
Now we are facing a serious problem for the cereal and oilseed crop farmers as well. The task force is making recommendations to the Minister for action in that area. We have made the commitment to assist the western Canadian farmers regarding the drought and we will. At the same time, the payments have gone out under the Western Grain Stabilization Act because of amendments that were made in this House. Crop insurance has been adjusted so that payments and adjustments can be made quickly. The Government has acted in a number of other areas of legislation that has been brought before this House. I find the arguments made by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) to be pretty weak.
Not so many years ago, I sat in the spot of the Hon. Member for Algoma. It was much easier to criticize than to defend. The Hon. Member visited the drought areas. I would ask him if he made observations, decided on possible solutions and mailed those solutions to the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson). I see his head shaking in the negative. Therefore, we have not heard his suggestions as to how that assistance might be offered. We have only heard criticism. At any rate, I know that suggestions we will hear will be adequate and the farmers will be pleased with the assistance that will be offered in the next few weeks.
I wish to make some comments on the Seeds Act. The Seeds Act is very important to farmers across the country. Canada can be proud of the legislation that has allowed proper research to take place into the various varieties of seeds that have been offered to Canadian farmers. The legislation has put before us a system of which we can be proud, a system that takes seeds from the research centres and puts them in the hands of farmers so that farmers can take that progeny and expand on it so that it can be made available very quickly to ordinary commercial seed growers or farmers. That is something of which we have to be very proud. That Act was brought in, I believe, back in 1905. It was written with such thought at the time that few amendments have had to be made up to this point in time. A minor amendment was made in 1977. As the Minister has stated, we are now attempting to adjust the Seeds Act in a mainly technical manner to ensure that it will be more beneficial to farmers than it is at the present time.
I have no argument with most of the sections of the Act. However, I do have an argument with one in particular. I wish to raise that matter in my short address to the House this afternoon. I approve of the amendments which are being proposed to many of the sections which have to do with the importation of seeds, the bonding of importers and the seizure of improper seeds coming into the country. The penalties which were originally brought in in 1905 are outdated at this
September 12, 1985

time. They need to be adjusted so that farmers will take them more seriously. The status of the Canadian Seed Growers Association is also dealt with in this legislation.
However, as is often the case when departments draft Bills of this type, it is possible for them to put into the legislation powers with which I have some concern and with which many legislators would have concern, if they were to give it some deep thought. We were warned of the possibility of changes to the manner in which farmers may be able to advertise seeds in this country because the legislation which is before us now has been talked about for some years. Those of us who represent grain-growing areas have consulted with our seed growers and with commercial farmers as to whether or not they have had any difficulties with the legislation. 1 sent out hundreds of letters in my constituency to farmers who produce grain and seed asking for their comments. Most of them commented in favour of the legislation with the exception of one section.
That section has to do with Clause 4(2) of the Bill wherein a number of powers are being added by regulation. The one that is of most concern is that with respect to the advertising of seeds. Under the present legislation, it is only possible for a registered seed grower to use the term "registered seed" or "certified seed". Usage of those terms signifies that the grower has a licence to take progeny from the agricultural research stations or scientists at universities who produce such seed, expand it and make it available in true variety to farmers. However, in the past, under the Act, farmers who have purchased registered seed have been allowed to grow that seed and advertise it as commercial seed grown from registered seed. For example, Johnson barley which is purchased as registered Johnson barley is grown on a commercial farm and then offered for sale in advertisement as commercial seed grown from registered Johnson barley. Many seed growers have stated that there is the possibility that a farmer looking in a newspaper without proper scrutiny will think that he is buying true variety. That is generally not the case since most commercial farms are not as cautious as they should be with respect to ensuring that the fields they plant of this true variety are free of other varieties. Thus, I can see the reasoning for putting forward such an amendment. However, I believe the point has been carried too far.
The reason I believe it has been carried too far is that the legislation now states that no farmer shall be able to advertise a variety of crop for sale but that he will only be able to advertise, for example, barley for sale, oats for sale or wheat for sale. 1 can imagine if I were a farmer that I would want to purchase not registered seed from a registered seed grower but a commercial seed, perhaps because my crop froze last year, 1 do not have the seed available and I need to purchase seed for my whole farm. Registered seed generally sells at $1 to $3 a bushel above commercial seed. To buy seed for hundreds or even thousands of acres can be extremely expensive if only registered seed is bought. Thus, many farmers who make a practice of buying commercial seed are not concerned about it being 100 per cent true to variety. They are concerned about getting as true a seed as possible in the ground in the spring.
Seeds and Grain Acts
Therefore, they buy from neighbouring farms a variety which they believe is close to true and has a good germination factor. It is important that we continue to allow commercial seed growers to advertise the variety name. I hope I can convince the Minister and the officials when we meet in committee that we should not allow commercial seed growers to use the term "grown from registered seed" or "grown from certified seed", but that they can continue to use the variety name.
The point I am making is a very narrow but important one. It is important to many farmers. I speak from the experience of western Canada; however, I am sure the case can be made across the country. I believe, then, that there will be adequate distinction between certified seed or registered seed and seed which is grown on a commercial farm. That would make it much easier, in the early spring, when most farmers are looking for seed for their farms, to go down the advertising columns in search of seed. For example, if I am looking for Johnson barley for my farm I will be able to see whom I have to call to inquire about the seed because it will be listed as Johnson barley. I will also know that it is not registered or certified and that it is not intended to be totally true to variety and that there may be some possibility of wheat seeds present in the sample.
I hope to bring this issue with some vigour and backing by my constituents to the legislative committee so that we can receive an indication from the Minister and his officials as to why he feels it improper to continue to use the variety name. I hope that we will hear not only from the registered seed growers but from the commercial farmers as well with respect to the difficulties this suggested amendment will cause. Perhaps we can come to a compromise amendment which will be of assistance to farmers when they are attempting to purchase seed in the spring.
You will find, Mr. Speaker, that there are many times more commercial growers in Canada than registered seed growers. They do produce a relatively good sample for farmers and over the last century many, many farmers in Canada have utilized the commercial seed grower and have received good results from that seed. I also commend the registered seed growers who have served this country well. They are very diligent in their practice of providing adequate and true seed for farmers. They have abided very well, in large, by the act over the last number of years. Therefore, I support the Bill with the exception of that section. I intend to raise it in committee. I am pleased that we are dealing with this very important Bill in such a proper and concise manner today.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to comment on the speech of the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellen-berger) because he really tried to lead the House to believe that the Government was taking very substantive action with regard to agriculture. I was amazed because it seems to me that we essentially have had a tremendous stall on any number of issues facing agriculture. The Bill today, although it is important in a technical sense and beneficial to the registered

September 12, 1985
Seeds and Grain Acts
seed growers and to the commerce of that whole industry, is surely not as important as the other issues facing agriculture in Canada today, such as the drought in western Canada.
The Hon. Member asked what the Liberals would do. Last year we made a commitment in the Mackenzie area of northeastern Saskatchewan of some $20 per acre. Perhaps it should now be $25 and the provincial Government should match it. However, when we were in power we made that kind fo commitment late in July. It is now getting into the middle of September and the Government still has not made any commitment for the grain industry even though it is facing a desperate situation.
I would like to read briefly in a report from a newspaper article in which the Saskatchewan wheat pool calls for $.5 billion program in drought aid. The proposal would involve payments up to $50 an acre to farmers in the most severely affected areas. Mr. Avery Sahl, the vice-president of the Saskatchewan pool said that even $50 an acre will barely be enough to help the most drastically affected to survive, particularly producers who spent thousands of dollars fighting grasshoppers this summer. Mr. Sahl is also a member of the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee. He said that 30,700 Saskatchewan farms have been affected by the drought in varying degrees.
I think the most important part of the article is Mr. Sahl's comment with regard to farm families because the drought is one thing with the loss of crops and so on but the impact on the families is equally important. He went on to say, and I quote:
Some farm families are literally destitute in our part of the province,... Others are not far behind, and the communities which rely on agriculture are severely strained.
In a major portion of the province, the whole rural economy is bordering on collapse.
Therefore I believe that urging the Government to make a decision and take action now is not out of line. I am sure that sentiment is echoed by every western producer who wants to see the Government take action.
The Hon. Member says that the Government is bringing forward a lot of substantial legislation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) published a paper in January and gave his views of Canadian agriculture. He put out a white paper on taxation issues in agriculture and said essentially in that paper that farmers were well off, they made twice as much money as the average Canadian and paid a quarter as much tax. I question and I believe every farmer in this country questions whether that is not really the philosophy of the Government. I am not speaking about the backbenchers because the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) was a very active Member on the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. He made some very worth-while recommendations and suggestions to the committee. However, what happened to them? With respect to the farm debt crisis, which is certainly worse than in the 1930s, no action has been taken, even though the farm debt crisis has exacerbated. The number of farmers in serious financial difficulty has risen from 17 per
cent or 19 per cent last year-depending on how you calculate-to 20 per cent of the farmers in Canada today. For the Hon. Member to suggest the Government is bringing forward momentous decisions is really not true because those decisions are not there for the farm debt crisis. Certainly no decision has been made on the red meat stabilization plan. One of the decisions which was made in the Budget was to assist farmers to get out of farming. Another decision was to impose a nine cent a gallon excise tax on fuel. That was a major campaign commitment just a little over a year ago when the Conservative Party were on the hustings. Within nine months of taking that tax off fuel, they imposed a tax of nine cents a gallon which in the West is being called the harvest tax. On June 1, they removed the exemption on the petroleum compensation charge which was another six cents or seven cents a gallon. In the last three months, therefore, the Government has really imposed some 15 cents or 16 cents a gallon fuel tax. A year from January it will be imposing another four cents a litre or 18 cents a gallon of new tax. Surely that is not the kind of dramatic action about which the Hon. Member spoke because it just exacerbates the situation and imposes that much more hardship because of the increase in farm input costs.
The Hon. Member says the Government is taking action in bringing forward legislation. We have not seen a decision on the dairy policy or on the farm debt crisis. We have a debate going on between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) as to whether they are going to put in place a prebankruptcy or preforeclosure arbitration procedure. We know the Budget of the Department of Agriculture is going to be cut by some $50 million but we do not know what that is going to affect. We have seen worse kinds of difficulties with trade issues in this past 12 months than farmers have faced in many years. We are supposed to have a new era in our relationship with the United States and other countries but all we see is something like a thousand carcasses of EEC subsidized beef being dumped into our Canadian market. We see a countervail on hogs going to the United States of 5.3 cents a pound. I would like to believe the Hon. Member. I know he is a dedicated and committed Member, one who has worked very effectively in the committee on farm legislation, but I really do not see this dramatic and effective legislation coming forward which he talked about when he spoke this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has a selective memory, and that is allowed when you are in opposition. Perhaps it is typical. He ought to make it clear that the reason they acted so quickly in July of last year was because there was an election on and it became very important to offer quickly a supposed solution to the drought situation. We have acted quickly, as I said in my speech, with the $48 million allotment for cattle, and we will act, after full consultation, for the grain farmers in western Canada. He knows and I know that in the committee we dealt with the financial paper and we pointed out many of the errors. We made recommendations which I think are adequate and proper for farming, and some

As his Party's agriculture critic the Hon. Member has been very busy this year. The reason for that is that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has been very busy in acting for farmers across this country. I hope the Hon. Member continues to be very busy.
