speechtext:
My colleague issues a minor caution. I thank him again for his kind comments this morning.
I am pleased at this point to open the debate on second reading of Bill C-67 and Bill C-68, and I want to deal with each of them in turn. At the heart of Bill C-67 are important amendments to the Parole Act and the Penitentiary Act which will effect changes to the correctional program and conditional release known as mandatory supervision. Provisions in the Bill

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
will tighten some of the features of that program for penitentiary inmates who pose a high risk of violence. These changes are clearly required and they have long been advocated by police, victims' organizations, and many concerned private and professional groups and individuals. At the same time the Bill contains balancing provisions which will ensure that inmates who are considered good risks while under supervision in the community will be considered by the National Parole Board at the earliest possible point in their sentence.
In its first Speech from the Throne the Government expressed its intention to respond to public concerns with regard to our system of criminal justice. We promised to correct defects in that system to ensure the best protection of the public from criminal acts which can be devised. Bill C-67 is not the total answer to that promise but it is a very important beginning. It contains measures which were urgently required and could be introduced quickly while awaiting the outcome of broader policy reviews currently under way in my Ministry and in the Department of Justice.
Perhaps the most pressing matter dealt with by this Bill is that aspect of the existing law which compels the automatic release of penitentiary inmates on mandatory supervision as a result of earned remission. The law now allows an inmate to earn the remission of up to one-third of his sentence through good conduct. An inmate who has earned all of his earned remission must by law now be released after serving two-thirds of his sentence. The last third is served in the community under mandatory supervision. Such a release must be granted even if there is a consensus among correctional and parole officials that he poses an imminent risk of violence to the community. Situations such as this have occurred in the past, too often with tragic results. We on this side of the House find it abhorrent that this situation shoud be allowed to continue. That is why a mechanism was provided in this Bill to give the National Parole Board the authority to prevent releases in certain cases.
The schedule to the Bill identifies a group of offences which, by their nature, involve violent conduct. Inmates serving a sentence for one of those offences will no longer be unconditionally entitled to release on mandatory supervision. Their earned remission will be used to calculate a presumptive release date but they will be liable to have their release on mandatory supervision denied if certain other conditions are met.
I would digress here to say that where the Government enumerates lists of offences like this, there is certainly room for debate and discussion about the list, whether the number of offences it lists is too long or too short, and we are prepared to listen with an open mind when this matter goes to committee. However, we feel it is important that the House give guidance to the parole service for some of those offence where it is clear that an individual has been involved in violence in the past, where there is a potential for violence in the future, to ensure that before potentially violent criminals are released back into society the NPB has an opportunity to review those cases. Correctional officials will examine these cases, Mr. Speaker,
when the presumptive release data draws near. They will determine if, in addition, serious harm, which is defined in the Bill, or death, was caused to another person in the commission of the offence. If this criterion is also met, it will then be decided if there appears to be reasonable grounds to believe that another offence causing serious harm or death would be committed while under mandatory supervision if that person were released. Should such grounds appear to exist the case will be referred to the National Parole Board. This is a mechanism to trigger a review by the NPB to ensure the rights of ordinary, innocent, law-abiding Canadians, their right to be free from violence, are respected. The Board will review background and other information that is material to the case, including the assessment of experts where necessary. A hearing will be held at which the inmate will be able to make representations on his own behalf. Procedural safeguards will be provided throughout this process so that the inmate is aware of the information being considered by the Board, is able to present his own case and be assisted at the hearing, and is aware of the reasons for the decision that is ultimately taken by the Board.
Time limits are prescribed in the Bill and others will be contained in the regulations. These will ensure that, barring exceptional circumstances, the process will allow enough time before the presumed release date for the inmate to apply for a re-examination of the decision by a different panel of Parole Board members, and to apply to the Federal Court for a review if he feels that he is not being treated fairly.
Following its review and hearing the Board will decide if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the inmate would commit an act of violence while under mandatory supervision. If so, the Board will be empowered to order that the inmate not be so released and remain in the penitentiary until the expiry of the full sentence or until the detention order is lifted. Lifting the order would reinstate the balance of the mandatory supervision period. Should the Board decide that it would only be safe to release an inmate under strict conditions, it would be able to require such conditions to be met before allowing the release to take place. These conditions could include residence in a community-based residential facility operated under a private or public auspices, including low security penitentiary facilities usually referred to as community correction centres. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, these measures will enable us to fill a gap by providing the correctional system with the possibility of singling out potentially dangerous inmates and preventing their release on parole, or of releasing them under mandatory supervision under very strict conditions.

They will do so while fully protecting the rights of inmates not to be treated arbitrarily or capriciously where their liberty is at stake. While it would be vain to hope that all potentially dangerous inmates can be identified, or that all violence by released inmates can be prevented, these measures will ensure
September 12, 1985

that we are able to effectively intervene when there are reasonable grounds to anticipate violent conduct during the sentence that it is our responsibility to administer. Although the number of such cases may be few, the additional protection this will offer to the public will be significant.
1 think it is appropriate for me to digress briefly at this point to say that I am new to my responsibilities and am looking forward to having a chance to learn more about them as 1 go along. 1 am not a lawyer, as was mentioned at the time 1 was appointed. 1 am new to the criminal justice system. I hope that on behalf of the people of Canada I will be able to bring a fresh perspective to the criminal justice system. Most importantly, I hope to be able to represent some of the concerns that are felt by ordinary Canadians with regard to violent crime. What is significant to me, Mr. Speaker, and to the people that each of us in the House of Commons represents, is that in a democracy like ours the most basic liberty that we have is the freedom from violent crime. The most basic responsibility that each of us has as a member of this House is to speak up on behalf of innocent Canadians, people who are guilty of no crimes, people whose lives or safety could be placed in danger if we were not to act.
It is always essential in any measures which are taken in the field of correctional institutions or penal law that there be checks and balances put in place to ensure the basic civil liberties of all people in the system. We believe that these measures in no way derogate from that responsibility, but we believe as well that it is essential to never forget that our most basic responsibility is to assure innocent people the freedom from violent crime. As long as I am Solicitor General of Canada that will remain my highest priority. I make that undertaking to the people who we represent.
The second major feature of this Bill also applies to those inmates identified by the first criterion I have mentioned, that is, conviction for one of the offences contained in the schedule to the Bill. Inmates falling into this category who are not found to pose an imminent risk of violence, and who are released on mandatory supervision, will be given only one chance to succeed. If that first release is revoked for any reason, be it a new offence or breach of a condition, they will not be released on mandatory supervision again during that sentence.
At the present time inmates who have their mandatory supervision revoked begin to earn remission again as soon as they are readmitted to penitentiary. They may, therefore, sometimes be released more than once during the same sentence leading to what has been termed the "revolving door syndrome". It is difficult to justify the risk of giving inmates, who have committed violent crimes and then demonstrated an inability to successfully readjust to the responsibilities of the free community, more than one such opportunity.
We accept that society at large must take risks and that our goal must be the rehabilitation of people convicted of offences under the law. However, we also have the responsibility to provide for the protection of the public at large. Having given that opportunity to someone who has been convicted of a
Criminal Code Amendments
serious offence, the onus is then on him or her to prove worthy of the trust which society has vested in them.
The foregoing elements of the Bill are designed to deal more effectively with inmates who are judged to pose an exceptional danger to the public. The third major component is, on the other hand, aimed at those who are considered to be exceptionally good risks. The Bill will require the Parole Board to review and grant a hearing in person to every inmate earlier in his sentence than at present. This will not alter existing limits on parole eligibility in any way. It will only require that the Parole Board grant a full review and hearing in every case when the first eligibility date is reached. This will occur, in most cases, after one-sixth of the sentence is served, rather than one-third as is now the case. By these means the best risks can be identified and granted some form of conditional release as early as possible consistent with public protection. Even those who are not considered ready for release will be given guidance early in their sentence as to what is expected of them so that if they choose, they can begin to work toward the objectives that will lead to their eventual conditional release.
I believe that taken together these measures form a balanced package that should lead to a more rational correctional system that directs scarce resources to where they are most needed, namely the more secure and more costly environment of the penitentiary for those who pose a high risk of violence, and supervised community based programs for those who pose a low risk of violence and a higher likelihood of a successful return to the community and to a law-abiding lifestyle.
The balancing and rationalizing character of this Bill is very important to avoid unacceptable human and monetary costs while protecting the safety of the public and the rights of offenders. It was astonishing to me to discover, upon becoming Solicitor General, that today it costs on average over $40,000 a year for every inmate maintained in a penitentiary whereas it costs just over $4,000 to supervise one parolee in the community. Moreover, many argue that the longer one spends in prison the more difficult is his eventual transition back to the community.
On both grounds, correctional and fiscal, it makes good sense to discriminate as effectively as possible. The good risks who stand the best chance of a successful return to society should be placed in community programs as early as possible with all the support and supervision that they require. The high risks who are potentially dangerous should, on the other hand, be kept in secure custody as long as they are under sentence. These measures will help us to do so more effectively than is the case at present.
Some critics of the correctional system have advocated the simple abolition of mandatory supervision because of its purported failure. The huge costs of such a proposal and the relative success of the program make it clear that this would not be a justifiable option at this time. Abolition of mandatory supervision or, in other words, the elimination of release due to earned remission, would effectively increase by one-third the sentence length of all inmates serving a definite term and not

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
release on full parole. Such a categorical approach would punish the deserving along with the undeserving. About 3,000 inmates would be affected each year, half of whom now complete mandatory supervision successfully. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it could lead to the construction of as many as six new penitentiaries at a capital cost of about $50 million each in addition to millions of dollars in annual operating expenses.
Those who would argue that this is a justifiable cost in view of the protection that it offers often do not recognize that of the 50 per cent who have their mandatory supervision revoked, about half or 25 per cent of the total have committed no new offence, but have simply broken a condition. In these cases the revocation is a preventative measure taken by the Parole Board to avoid the commission of a crime as the end result of deteriorating adjustment of the parolee. Indeed, of the total number of inmates released on mandatory supervision, 25 per cent commit a new offence while still under sentence but only 2.7 per cent commit an offence involving violence and another 3.3 per cent commit robbery; for a total of 6.6 per cent of the total if we lump these two categories together.
The costs and the inequities involved in such a categorical approach outweigh the benefits and has therefore been rejected. In my view, the measures contained in Bill C-67 make such better sense since they are aimed at identifying those inmates from whom society clearly requires protection, and in providing mechanisms for protection from them for as long as legally possible while not interfering with the majority who give no indication of posing an exceptionally high risk.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think that the measures I have just outlined will enable us to correct some of the most obvious and criticized deficiencies of the present system of parole under mandatory supervision. Yet they will not in any way curtail the rights of inmates, no more than they will unfairly penalize those inmates who are obviously not prone to violence.
They will offer Canadians better protection against delinquents who can rightfully be expected to resort to violence, yet without having to dramatically increase expenditure as would be the case if we were to apply such measures indiscriminately to all inmates.

I believe that it is a fair, rational and balanced package that I am eager to have reviewed in committee. I would also indicate today, as I did yesterday with Bill C-65, that there are provisions in the Bill which provide for the Governor in Council to make regulations. In those instances where that provision is included in the Bill, I will see to it that the Government moves a motion to insert the magic formula of "by order" to ensure those regulations are considered to be statutory instruments, are published and are made available to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. I have already received certain constructive representations from interested members of the
public and professional groups and welcome similar observations from Members of the House on whom I urge speedy passage of this much needed Bill.
Looking back on my own responsibilities as Minister of National Revenue and the measures which the Government took in terms of bringing down a declaration of rights for taxpayers for Canadians for the first time and measures we took to build into the Income Tax Act provisions to ensure that innocent people are treated with decency and respect, I think it demonstrates the commitment of the Government and perhaps all Members of Parliament to ensure that innocent people have their rights fully respected. We hope to continue that philosophy throughout my tenure as Solicitor General, to ensure that the rights of the accused are properly protected, that we recognize that they do have rights and those people who are incarcerated in penal institutions are fully respected as well.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), is in the House. I watched with interest on Sunday as he and his colleagues were leaving Mont St. Marie where they were having a meeting. The news media indicated that his Party would begin to reopen a theme that it used during the course of the last election campaign-speaking up for ordinary people. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is for ordinary people that all of us on both sides of the House must speak. I say in particular that I believe that the ordinary person is honest, that he is law abiding and innocent and he deserves to have his rights fully protected by the Government.

It is precisely for honest men and honest women that we are bringing in this legislation. We believe that the most basic right that any Canadian has-and it is nowhere more evident than in violence against women-is to be protected from violent crime. Mr. Speaker, allow me now to speak to Bill C-68 entitled an Act to amend the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prison and Reformatories Act and the Criminal Code.
Unlike the provisions of Bill C-67, these are housekeeping amendments designed to clarify the calculation and administration of sentences, and to facilitate the operations of the Correctional Service of Canada, the National Parole Board and the provincial correctional institutions.
September 12, 1985



The last significant amendments to the Parole Act, Penitentiary Act and Prisons and Reformatories Act were made in 1977. Oversights made at that time, changing circumstances and concerns that have arisen with experience require amendments to clarify, consolidate and correct the statutes.
Some of the amendments proposed in Bill C-68 have appeared with more substantive amendments in previous Bills which were not adopted by Parliament. Many of the amendments reflect longstanding concerns of provincial Governments which we are pleased to be able to rectify. All of the amendments are designed to correct oversights and deficiencies in the correctional law statutes, and contribute to the efficient, orderly and fair operation of federal and provincial correctional programs.
I would like to highlight for the House examples of the type of amendments which we are proposing under each Act. First,
I refer to the Parole Act, which provides for the calculation of sentences for inmates in federal penitentiaries, as well as for the release of these inmates on parole or under mandatory supervision. Since its proclamation in 1959, the Parole Act has been subjected to periodic amendments, largely initiated in response to immediate pressures and events. The Board has grown from five decision-makers to close to 100 permanent and temporary members; from a centralized establishment in Ottawa to one stretching from Vancovuer to Moncton; from the provision of parole reviews on paper, to hearings providing an array of procedural safeguards; from almost no judicial scrutiny, to a heavy caseload of litigation. In many cases, correctional authorities are attempting to cope with the current situation with an inadequate and out of date framework of legislation and regulations. The amendments to the Parole act contained in Bill C-68 do not attempt to address long-term problems, problems which are now undergoing comprehensive review. Rather, these amendments address urgent and long delayed matters of technical but nonetheless significant concern.
Of primary concern with respect to the Parole Act which Bill C-68 addresses is that of ensuring that sentences of inmates confined in federal penitentiaries are calculated so as to accurately reflect the intent of the judge who sentenced the offender. Section 14 of the Parole Act was originally enacted to facilitate the administration of sentences by correctional authorities. The section attempts to achieve that purpose by deeming different terms of imprisonment which were imposed either at the same sittings of court or at separate occasions, and for which there would normally be different parole eligibility dates and release dates, to constitute one single sentence for which there is only one parole eligibility date and one release date. I emphasize that the deeming provision does not modify the duration of the sentences imposed by the courts.

I was hoping that my hon. friend would ask me to explain because I have done my homework on that. The concern we are trying to address with this particular provision

arose from an instance where an individual received two separate sentences for two separate offences. As a result of a provision in the law which was a technicality, the courts found that this individual, between the completion of his incarceration for his first sentence and incarceration for his second sentence, was allowed out on parole in the meantime. It was a provision which, on its face, made very little sense. Although it is not a problem which has cropped up regularly throughout Canada, we felt it was something that should be addressed to ensure that we would not have the anomaly of an individual being released as a result of a technicality in the law in between the serving of two prison sentences for offences which had already taken place, already been tried by the courts and for which he had already been sentenced to prison. Can 1 give my hon. friend any further elaboration?

That may exhaust my knowledge of it, anyway.
The single sentence it creates begins on the earliest day on which any of those sentences commenced and ends on the final day of the last to expire.
Although there is no doubt that Section 14 has been of great assistance in the administration of the majority of sentences, as I have already stated, its present wording suffers from certain shortcomings which limit its application and prevent correctional authorities from giving the full and proper effect of sentences imposed by the courts.
For example, under the present Section 14, situations have arisen where a judge has sentenced an offender to a substantial term of imprisonment only to find that the offender is immediately eligible for, or indeed is released on, parole due to the effect of combining the new sentence with the old. Such anomalous results are a source of great concern both to the public and to correctional authorities, and appropriate amendments are contained in Bill C-68 to correct these unintended effects in sentence calculation.
Now we get to the really meaty elements of the Bill. I know my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby will be anxious to follow this with fascination.
Other amendments to the Parole Act will not so much correct oversights as they will simply eliminate redundancies and obsolete provisions. For example, the definition of "magistrate" will be deleted. The substantive section to which it related was repealed by previous legislation. Similarly, portions of the Penitentiary Act will be transferred to the Parole Act, so that all matters pertaining to the jurisdiction of the National Parole Board will be found under one statute.
Some of the amendments will facilitate the day to day operations of the National Parole Board by clarifying certain sections of the Parole Act. For example, amendments to Section 3 of the Act will clarify the authority of the Executive Committee of the Board to vote on parole hearings or reviews. Other amendments will provide specific regulation-making

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
authority for certain matters, instead of the current statutory structure which provides only a general "basket clause" to authorize the enactment of regulations. This can, at times, leave in doubt the authority to enact certain regulations.
The second group of amendments in Bill C-68 pertain to the Penitentiary Act, the Act which provides for the administration of federal penitentiaries. Again, these amendments do not embody substantive changes in policy, but rather attempt to correct some long-standing technical problems.
I know that my colleague from Burnaby has long been vexed by the question of the name of the Canadian Penitentiary Service. For that reason, we will be changing that name to the Correctional Service of Canada. This will reflect in statute the amalgamation of the Canadian Penitentiary Service and the National Parole Service. This amalgamation took place eight years ago. This long overdue amendment for which the Hon. Member has fought long and hard will permit the official use of the designation "Correctional Service of Canada", which has been used in practice since 1977.
Similarly, another amendment will designate all officers and employees of Correctional Service Canada as "members" of the service. The 1960 Penitentiary Act referred to the two former categories of employees of the service, however, the basis for this distinction has completely disappeared with time. Confusion has resulted in the continued reference to the two categories in the Act, which this amendment will now resolve.
A related amendment will restrict the designation of peace officer status to only those members of the service so designated by the Commissioner of Corrections. Under the current legislation, all officers of the service are automatically designated as peace officers. Such a sweeping provision in our view, is unnecessary and in some cases counter-productive for those members of the service engaged in rehabilitation, rather than strictly custodial functions.
While amendments such as these are designed to facilitate the operation of the Correctional Service of Canada, other amendments will have a more direct impact on inmates in assisting their reintegration into society. For example, a section will be added to the Act to enable an offender who has been released on parole or under mandatory supervision to be lodged, temporarily and at his or her own request, in a penitentiary. This provision is considered desirable primarily during times when an offender may be experiencing difficulty while on conditional release. This would provide the offender with a short period of relief when the stress of returning to society may be compelling him or her to less constructive options for coping.

Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-68 features several amendments to the Prisons and Reformatories Act. This federal legislation deals with questions of administration of sentences to be served by inmates of provincial correctional institutions. There are close ties between federal and provincial jurisdictions with respect to the implementation of correctional programs and I am pleased about the excellent spirit of cooperation between the provincial Governments at the operational level when there is interaction between the institutions and the probation and parole programs.
As well, we share a number of common endeavours with the provinces and we work in close cooperation with them in such fields as crime prevention and assistance services to victims of criminal acts.

In this light, Bill C-68 contains amendments to the Prisons and Reformatories Act to deal with a variety of provincial requests, some of which have been outstanding for many years. In the coming months, suggestions for additional amendments to the Act will also be considered. Throughout these activities we will seek to reduce to a minimum any unnecessary involvement in provincial corrections while seeking mutually beneficial joint action.
As one example of the amendments proposed by Bill C-68 in this regard, provincial correctional authorities have requested a clarification in statute of the status of inmates while they are temporarily outside the correctional institution. This would include, for example, inmates on work details outside the institution or inmates who require emergency medical treatment at a hospital. In consequence, we are proposing a new section in the Act which would clarify that such inmates are in custody for the purposes of this Act and any other Act of Parliament.
Some of the amendments to this statute deal more with terminology. For example, the use of terms "rules" and "regulations" will be made consistent throughout the Act. The repeal of obsolete provisions relating to the forfeiture of statutory remission will reflect previous changes made to the Act as long ago as 1978.
An amendment to Section 10 of the Act will change the terminology of the section to accord with the terminology and age provisions of the Young Offenders Act. The provisions for holding young persons separately from adults in provincial institutions will also be made consistent with the Young Offenders Act.
Fourth, one amendment will be made to the Criminal Code in consequence of the amendment to the Penitentiary Act respecting the limited designation of certain members as peace officers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe that these proposed amendments embody a number of long-needed clarifications and corrections to the statutes in question. Their timely passage through this House will facilitate the fair and efficient administration of the federal and provincial correctional systems.
These two Bills represent an important beginning in the Government's efforts to rationalize and modernize correctional programs. They deal with some of the most pressing and apparent problems. I am confident they will lead to a more efficient system and more secure environment for all Canadians.
September 12, 1985

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to rise on debate of these two Bills that have been grouped, Bill C-67 and Bill C-68. I intend in the course of my remarks on these Bills to address initially the question of the underlying objectives set out by the Minister in these Bills. I intend to focus, I might say, on Bill C-67. While a number of the subjects addressed by the Minister in his learned discourse on Bill C-68 were obviously of vital concern, I believe the issues raised by Bill C-67 are so fundamental and so important in the criminal justice system that I intend to focus my remarks on Bill C-67.
I will briefly go through the background objectives of Bill C-67, Mr. Speaker. I propose then to examine the history of mandatory supervision, what it was that lead to mandatory supervision, how it has worked in practice and briefly touch upon some of the studies that have been done in terms of the effectiveness of mandatory supervision, and mention concerns that have been raised by the community and by prisoners. I will then turn to the changes proposed by the Minister to the system of mandatory supervision. In fact, there are two major areas of change dealing with what has been called the revolving door syndrome, and as well institutionalizing a system of what has been called gating.
I intend to deal with what we in this Party believe to be some very serious problems with the Minister's proposals in these areas. I intend to set out in some detail our concerns with respect to their proposals. Finally, in the time remaining, I hope to be able to discuss alternatives which we in the New Democratic Party have for dealing with what is a very legitimate and real concern on the part of the community with respect to violence, in particular to the victims of crime who are too often overlooked in our system of criminal justice.
As I said, the purpose of this Bill is set out, and was clearly set out by the Minister, to address the concern of the community respecting the revolving door syndrome, that is the syndrome whereby prisoners who are on mandatory supervision may have their mandatory supervision revoked, be returned to prison, serve a period of time, come out, have their mandatory supervision revoked, go back and so on. The first objective of the Bill is to put an end to that and to provide, where mandatory supervision is revoked, that there will be no further remission of sentence. The second and very important objective of the Bill is the provision which in effect would grant a sweeping new power to the National Parole Board to designate certain individuals, at the time they become eligible for mandatory supervision, as individuals who should be denied their liberty, denied mandatory supervision and held, in effect, until the remainder of their term.
I suppose one could ask what is objectionable about those provisions or what we feel is harmful about provisions which,
Criminal Code Amendments
on their face, appear to be in accord with the concerns of the community. It will be my submission that far from responding in a real way to the concerns of the community, the Bill really provides an illusion of security and an illusion of safety to the community when in fact precisely the opposite will be the effect. I am not only speaking on my own behalf and on behalf of members of my caucus. However, I think it is fair to say that it is virtually the unanimous view of those who are active in the criminal justice system and the correctional service, barring, I might say, the police. I believe it is only the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police which advocated these sweeping measures. All others, particularly those involved in after-care, including the John Howard Society, the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Crime, the Elizabeth Fry Society and so on, have condemned this approach.
Why have they condemned it? They have condemned it because instead of reducing the level of violent crime in our communities, the approach which is being taken by the Government will in fact increase that level and will increase the danger to those innocent men and women about whom the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) spoke earlier. The proposals will result in a dramatic increase in the population of our federal prison system at a time when that system is already seriously overcrowded. Not only will that overcrowding lead to significantly increased tension in the prison system, which makes it more difficult for prison guards and results in increased violence, both prisoner to prisoner and also with respect to those who work in the institutions, but it will lead to a significant increase in cost to Canadian taxpayers. I would have thought that the Government would have looked more closely at this proposal before recommending to Parliament a scheme which will dramatically increase the cost to Canadians of operating the federal penitentiary system. My friend, the Solicitor General, has already pointed out that it costs some $40,000 per year to incarcerate a prisoner in that federal system. Indeed, it costs about $120,000 to build a new prison cell. One must contrast that to a cost of some $3,000 or $3,500 per year for after-care out in the community.
I have mentioned the concerns with respect to an increase in danger to our community, an increase in violent crime, the problem of overcrowding and the problem of a greatly increased budget for prisons. As well I would note that this proposal will result in reducing the good behaviour incentive for prisoners within the federal prison system. In effect it cuts back substantially on earned remission. The reality is that there will be an air of insecurity within the institutions. It is for that reason that prison wardens recommended against the kind of proposal which is being put forward by the Solicitor General to Parliament. The views of prison wardens in this area, those who are on the front lines, so to speak, should be given very careful consideration. Certainly they should be invited to appear before the legislative committee which will study this matter.
Finally, this Bill will do a profound injustice to prisoners and to those who are serving sentences in the community. While it is often unpopular to speak of injustices to that community, we

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
must bear in mind the remarks of Windston Churchill many decades ago when he said in effect that the mark of civilization in a community was not how it treated the elite in its society or those in positions of privilege, but how it treated the poor, the downtrodden sand, in particular, how it treated prisoners.
In light of the concerns which I have outlined, I want to examine the proposals of the Government. There are two major thrusts to the Bill. First, it would allow the National Parole Board to refuse mandatory supervision to certain serious offenders who are perceived as a threat to the community. As it stands now, the granting of mandatory supervision is automatic as long as a prisoner has displayed good behaviour during his or her term of imprisonment. At the end of two thirds of the sentence, the granting of mandatory supervision is automatic. This Bill would remove that feature and allow the National Parole Board to attempt to predict future behaviour and to attempt to predict violence.
In seeking this new power from Parliament, the Government and the Solicitor General should bring forward some evidence to back up their suggestion that it is possible to predict violence. In the absence of such evidence, in the absence of evidence indicating that a national parole board or a quasijudicial body can in fact look at an individual prisoner and say on the basis of observing his or her record that it is in a position to predict violence, of course the Government's argument falls down. I suggest to the Solicitor General that no study, not just in Canada but anywhere else in the world, has shown that it is possible to predict violence in this manner. On this subject the former Liberal Solicitor General commissioned a very exhaustive study of mandatory supervision. A report was prepared and submitted to the Government in November 1980 by a committee which was chaired by Joan Nuffield. That report clearly recommended against any measures which would involve an attempt to predict violence. After an exhaustive review of the evidence and research studies, the report found that there was no basis to the suggestion that that could in fact be done.
There is a more fundamental and a more basic concern than the one to which I have just referred. This Bill overlooks the fact that while those who are predicted as possibly being violent can be held behind bars, they will not be held indefinitely. In fact, in many cases they will be released at the end of their sentences, more bitter and more antagonistic, not having been dealt with in terms of the threat which they pose. They will not be released in a gradual manner with some sort of assistance, but they will be released directly from prison, in some cases directly from maximum security prisons on to the street. That is a threat to our communities which is far greater than the existing system.
I intend in my remarks tomorrow, because I believe it is five o'clock, to continue by addressing some of our very serious concerns with respect to this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Gormley (The Battlefords-Meadow Lake) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING ABORTION PROCEDURES
speechtext:
that Bill C-226, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (abortion), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to rise today on behalf of many of my constituents of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake in northwestern Saskatchewan and many of my friends across Canada to address the issue of abortion in Canadian society. This issue has had an impact on many Canadians and has been a painfully divisive and often controversial subject. Abortion has divided emotions and opinions. It has pitted often extreme points of view against one another. Beyond this, abortion has resulted in at least 65,000 human beings not being born every year in Canada and the latest figures place the estimate at close to 80,000 abortions per year. In other words, every week, 1,500 unborn children are aborted in Canada.
Regardless of one's view, abortion profoundly affects lives, the lives of living Canadians and the lives of those who one day will live. It is one of the most important and compelling struggles facing all of us.
Abortion is a medical, ethical, legal and theological issue touching all facets of human existence. Above all, abortion is a political issue that must be addressed by politicians in this Parliament. It is my hope that in this Private Members' Hour, politicians can address this matter in a non-partisan, constructive fashion. It is for this reason that I have proposed Bill C-226 for discussion.
What does this Bill propose? Presently, under Section 251(4) abortion is illegal except in cases where the life or health of a woman may be endangered or may likely be endangered. Bill C-226 proposes to amend the legislation to remove the words "or health" from this particular provision. As a result, this would make abortion less available than it presently is. I hope that in this hour, we may have a discussion on this issue and that I may be able to say why I feel the Criminal Code should be amended to make abortion less available.
September 12, 1985

The legal background of abortion in Canada predates Confederation itself. In 1803 in what was later to become the Criminal Code, the law that governs Canada today, a prohibition on abortion existed. This traced its roots back to England in the year 1603 when British law originally codified centuries of convention, convention that had established that abortion was illegal, wrong and that society should not accept abortion as an alternative.
Section 251 of Canada's Criminal Code has remained essentially the same for all of these years. It remained the same until the year 1969. In that year, Canadian law was amended to add three subsections to Section 251 of the Criminal Code. The subsections allowed certain immunities from the illegal nature of abortion. Abortion was still illegal following the amendments of 1969 but it was permissible if it was performed in an accredited hospital by an accredited doctor with the approval of a therapeutic abortion committee if that committee has approved an abortion certificate. The certificate was to be approved because it would be proven to the therapeutic abortion committee that the mother's life or health was endangered or likely to be endangered.
Bill C-226 proposes to address the Section of this law that deals with the endangerment of health. What constitutes the meaning of health? Most of us would interpret a literal meaning of health to be a sense of physical well-being. If physical health were the interpretation, it would clearly specify the acceptability or non-acceptability of abortion. However, health has been interpreted in many different ways.
The Health and Welfare Committee of this Parliament, when it studied the amendments to the abortion legislation in 1969, began hearings into the suggested changes in 1967. Obviously I was not a Member of this House then but I have found that on March 13, 1968, the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare made its report to Parliament. At that time, there was concern expressed about the meaning of the word "health". A partial transcript of the Committee Report reads as follows:
There has been a great deal of concern over the definition of health in the proposed amendments and in the Committee's interim report... the Committee feels that a simple amendment to the proposed legislation should establish that a clear and direct serious threat to the mother's health must be present.
The fear of the committee at that time, a fear that was later borne out by Canadian legal and medical history, was that the word "health" could be interpreted in the same way as the World Health Organization interprets it. The WHO definition of health reads:
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
Health by that definition became a rather ambiguous description of what many of us would take to be physical health. In defining such a large parameter including areas of social well-being, the health provision made abortion more available. If health was well-being and if that well-being could be demonstrably proven to be threatened to a therapeutic abortion committee, an abortion would be granted by that committee.
Criminal Code
The Badgley Commission dealt with the question of therapeutic abortion committees. In testimony before the Badgley Commission, it was shown that up to 80 per cent of abortions were being approved for reasons other than physical health. Obviously this ambiguous meaning has come to allow an unacceptably high number of abortions per year.
Just how many abortions take place in Canada and just how many take place because of this ambiguous term "health"? It is obviously difficult to assess in a statistical way how many are allowed through the interpretation of health, but I think we can look at the over-all statistics. The Badgley Commission, using a system of averaging and survey, reported that before 1969, fewer than 10,000 abortions were performed per year in Canada. Since the amendments of 1969 and the inclusion of this controversial word "health", according to the 1982 census, there were 66,400 abortions performed that year. That is down slightly from the late and mid-1970s but on average, in excess of 65,000 abortions are performed per year. In some circles, it is estimated that if one takes into account the entire number of therapeutic abortions now being performed this year in Canadian hospitals, the number could indeed approach 80,000. In other words, every day that Canadians go to work, almost 400 pregnancies are ended.
Was this the intention of politicians back in 1969? The then Minister of Justice, now the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), is by all accounts, a very honourable man. The Prime Minister of the day was well regarded by Members of this House. Surely it could not have been the intention of the Leader of the Official Opposition who was the Minister of Justice at the time to allow, by an ambiguity, a law that would allow abortions to increase six and sevenfold, a law that in a sense became a loophole.
Both in committee and in debate on the floor of the House of Commons, many politicians thought that by defining life or health, they were being called upon to legalize a few hundred abortions that were being performed anyway. Many of these politicians considered that there were serious medical reasons and by putting the words "or health" in the particular legislation that they were simply making valid what had gone on for some time.
Also, we should take into account the context of the times. In the intervening years between 1967 and 1969, the argument, when one debated abortion, was largely women's rights competing against the rights of an undifferentiated mass of cells. That was the argument that was often heard in those times. Later on, I think we will see that both the terms of the argument and the magnitude and importance of that argument has changed somewhat in the intervening years.
In 1969, did politicians have insight? Did politicians envisage that by amending that particular legislation they would, in a sense, be opening that door to this number of abortions? Recently, a distinguished colleague from this House, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who was here in

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code
1969, addressed a meeting here in Ottawa. In that address the hon. gentleman, when speaking about 1969, said, and I quote:
Are we prepared to recognize that our laws must accord intrinsic worth and equal value to the life of every human being regardless of its stage of development or condition?
He went on on to say:
I believe that all Members agonized over this question. In the collective wisdom of the House, a law was passed. It is not perfect, and it has not worked perfectly. No one is totally satisfied with it.
The issue of abortion, as will be touched on doubtlessly by other speakers, often involves very separate but inter-related issues. I would like to deal briefly with three of them. The first is the viability of the foetus; or, when does life begin? The second issue is freedom of choice. The third issue is: Every child a wanted child. This is what I call the theory of wantedness.
With respect to the viability of the foetus, the perception and the reality of this question has probably changed most dramatically since the years 1967 to 1969 through the advent of medical and scientific research. One recalls the words of Bernard Nathenson, an American doctor who was one of the founders of the National Abortion Rights Action League of New York, who has since become an outspoken critic of abortion, after being a leading physician at the leading edge and performing a number of abortions. Dr. Nathenson spoke of what became the turning point for him. It was what is called the study of foetology. In foetology, physicians are able to perform surgery and do comprehensive medical work on a child who is still a foetus, who is legally not born, who is within the womb of its mother. Dr. Nathenson has recounted, often stirringly, about the large hospital where he performed abortions where, on one floor, physicians at the leading adge of foetology were doing research and treatment on children within the wombs of their mothers, while on the floor below Dr. Nathenson and his colleagues were performing abortions on foetuses who were at the same age of foetal development.
If we look at one single year, 30 babies in Canada were relieved of hydrocephalic pressure on the skull, a build-up of water at the base of the brain. This surgery is performed within the uterus, within the womb of the mother. We can look at something which has gone on for many years, that is, the practice of inter-uterine blood transfusions.
With respect to the point of when does life begin, we must look at the advances in genetics and the advances in work on the beginning of life itself. We see that there are separate chromosome and gene patterns. Based on a preponderance of medical evidence, it is clear that the question of viability, or the question of life, is no longer such a large and looming question as it was in 1969.
Another point I would like to deal with is the freedom of choice. If we think of life as really a collection of choices, with some moderation of restraint or constraint upon us, obviously, all of us in life would like to be free to make choices. The oldest example of this is the English jurist who spoke once about the right of free movement and the right to swing one's arm. One had an unfettered right to swing one's arm; but that
right ended at the precise point where the next fellow's nose began. The question of rights and freedom of choice presupposes that the right of one person shall not adversely affect the condition of others. That is a presupposition to any freedom of movement or freedom of choice. Obviously, if we accept that there is a question of life, then surely the right of one person to exercise a choice infringes upon the life of another.
The third point which I wish to touch upon briefly, given the well intentioned nature of this argument, is the theory of wantedness. A well respected group in Canada has as its motto on birth control and planning "Every child a wanted child". That, indeed, is well intentioned. However, the theory wantedness becomes profoundly disturbing when we look at it in the context of: What about the unwanted? Many people in society have not wanted women; and we see the hard work and the many miles ahead on getting true equality for women. We see the exploitive nature of wife battering, of pornography, of abuse against women, because some people do not believe they "want women" to the same extent as they may want others. In post-colonial America, people did not want blacks and that justified slavery. In a Europe of 45 years ago, Nazis did not want Jewish people. That was used as a justification for genocide. So I caution Hon. Members against the theory of wantedness.
If we remove from the Criminal Code Section 251, the section on health, and we leave only the endangerment of life as admissible grounds for abortion, is this acceptable? I believe it is acceptable because the endangerment of life is directly related to the question of physical health. If one's physical health is endangered to the extent that it would endanger a life, then abortion, in my opinion, should be allowed. In this respect, to simply leave the endangerment of life encompasses the original interpretation and meaning of physical health and, obviously, protecting the life of an adult person. If a law can be used to remove a healthy living foetus from a physically life-endangered woman, then medical attempts can be made to save both persons as independent persons. In the case of the foetus which does not survive, then it is, yes, an exercising of rights, but the right to life of a physically endangered adult.
The present abortion law is in need of clarification, definition and substance. In the debate today I think I can say on behalf of all Members of the House from all political Parties that we have philosophical differences. Many Members agree with my amendment. Some suggest an even more restrictive amendment to the present abortion laws. On the other hand, many of my colleagues do not agree with my amendment. They would suggest that abortion be made completely legal. It has not been my intention to further polarize public opinion, or opinion within this Chamber. Further, I do not want to inflame the emotions or temperaments of those who sit in Parliament. However, it is clear we must address this issue.
I ask today that Members think very carefully and thoroughly, not so much about the specifics of this Bill but the adequacy of our present abortion legislation. If this Bill is talked out, which in the parlance of Parliament means that by the end of this hour someone will still speak and, thus, relegate
September 12, 1985

this Bill to the bottom of the Order Paper-and I hope that someone would not be from my own political Party, but I know that it may well in fact happen-then this matter will not likely be heard again in this Parliament. I ask all Members, in conscience, to think carefully about the decision to talk out this Bill. I ask that this Bill be referred to the House of Commons Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. And if an Hon. Member believes that the Bill does not go far enough or should go further, it is in the forum of that committee that there will be an opportunity to examine and thoroughly study the existing legislation and this important issue.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, while opinions are certainly divergent and points of view differing, only Members of Parliament can address this most vital issue. By inaction we do a service to no one. By upholding the status quo, we allow an unacceptably high number of abortions to continue to be conducted every single day in this country. Failure to address this issue amounts to standing mute while lives are ruined. Let all Hon. Members of Parliament remember this.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING ABORTION PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy for the opportunity to speak on the motion which has been put forward by my most distinguished colleague. As he may remember, I spoke some months ago in March of this year on a motion not similar but which did deal with the matter of abortion. As I said at that time I did not believe that Private Members' Hour was the appropriate forum in which to discuss a matter which is so difficult and upon which there is a divergence of opinion within the Canadian community. I would suggest to my colleague, therefore, that while this issue is of great importance to the Canadian public, this particular time is not the appropriate time for its discussion.
I would urge my colleagues again to remember that no matter what their views on this issue of abortion, whether they hold to the view of enlarging the scope to enable women to have greater choice or whether they would wish to restrict, as my hon. colleague is suggesting, the right of women to an abortion, we as parliamentarians have a greater responsibility to ensure that there are appropriate educational and counselling facilities for the women of this country. We must put the emphasis on the prevention of unwanted pregnancies rather than having to deal with the situation once it occurs.
I believe my colleagues on all sides of the House would join with me in the belief that this issue has not been addressed fully and adequately. I know from my own experience, as I mentioned back in March, that there are many young people in our society today who do not fully understand the implications of sexuality and of pregnancy. They find themselves in the situation of being pregnant where it would be extremely difficult for them to go through with the pregnancy and, of course, they wish an abortion. I feel if we had greater emphasis on education within the schools, homes and other social institutions of this society and supported the community
Criminal Code
groups who focus on this need, we would be a lot further ahead.
I would have to speak today against the motion of my dear friend and colleague. 1 know we agree in many different areas but this, as he said himself, is an area that even within our own Party there are many different points of view. I guess 1 would disagree with my hon. friend on several points. First, with respect to the justice of the issue itself and, second, on the mood of Canadians with respect to this issue. First, my colleague is suggesting amendments to the Criminal Code which would delete the right of women to have an abortion if it would endanger their health and therefore restrict the rights of women to have an abortion to only those circumstances where there would be an endangerment to life itself. My mind goes back to situations which happened some time ago, before the liberalization of the law as it now stands and I believe that would indeed be a retrogressive step. From my own personal point of view, I would want to see in the future further changes made and that ultimately we could come to a situation where the issue of abortion is removed from the Criminal Code entirely because in my view the issue of whether to continue with a pregnancy or not is the right of the woman in consultation with her physician or others who may be able to provide her with advice and counselling. Ultimately it should be the woman herself who should make that decision. To further restrict what we have now in legislation seems to me to be a dreadful disservice to the women of this country.
I am sure Hon. Members are all aware of the kinds of cases in past history of women seeking abortions and not being able to have them under proper facilities and being subjected to the kitchen tables. I am sure we all remember the tragedies, the maiming and the deaths which resulted under that system. Surely, none of us want to go back to the antiquated system we used to have.
The issue of abortion is not only a woman's issue because I find that both men and women across the country are increasingly coming to support the right of women to make a decision on this issue. I am sure that many of my colleagues read the poll which was reported in June of this year in The Globe and Mail. It indicated that 53 per cent of those Canadians surveyed agreed that every woman who wants an abortion should be able to have one. An even larger majority thought the Government should ensure that there are abortion facilities in areas where hospitals do not currently perform abortions. In fact, that has been an issue raised in the Committee of Equality Rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which I had the honour to sit on. Our present legislation does not meet the criteria of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights because it does not provide equal accessibility to women throughout the country. I think the results of this survey of Canadians support the view that women should have accessibility to facilities in hospitals or in appropriate clinics in order to obtain safe abortions.
There are other interesting comments from this survey as well. When we look at the breakdown of the people who responded to the survey, it is interesting to note that among

September 12, 1985
Criminal Code
those with post-high school education, 62 per cent supported the freedom of choice position. That seems, in my opinion, to indicate that as people have the opportunity to become more familiar and more understanding of the issues involved, they are prepared to support the freedom of choice position. People in higher income groups and those living in larger communities tended to be more supportive of choice as well. I think that is understandable, knowing the make-up of Canada and the attitude of Canadians on this issue. The age group which is most likely to be personally affected by abortion, that is, women of 18 to 29 years, were also the most in favour. That is indicative that the women who are most affected by this issue understand and recognize that there should be freedom of choice. Fifty-eight per cent of those in that age group agreed with freedom of choice as compared with only 41 per cent of respondents over 60 years of age.
There was a further question as to when a woman should be able to obtain a legal abortion. Of those surveyed, 78 per cent thought it should be possible if the abortion had been approved by a therapeutic abortion committee, 87 per cent approved if the woman's health was in danger and 93 per cent approved if the woman's life was in danger. I believe one can see from that 87 per cent of those surveyed-and this was a poll taken right across the country-that a woman should be able to have an abortion if her health was in danger. Therefore I do not think the proposal my dear friend is putting forward is consistent with the general attitude of Canadians.
[DOT] (W30)
Finally, in this particular report there was something which I found very interesting and perhaps some of my colleagues are not aware of it. Religious differences on access to abortion were not as great as might be expected. Some 60 per cent of Protestants and 57 per cent of Catholics surveyed favoured increased access to abortion facilities. While more Protestants agreed that a woman should be able to obtain an abortion when she wanted one, a high percentage of Catholics, 57 per cent, also took this position. I think that indicates that this is not an issue divided purely on religious lines and we can take heart from that.
Recognizing the concerns in the community my friend represents, and the concerns of many Canadians that there should be some change in the law regarding abortions, I have to say to the Hon. Member that, while he is certainly not alone, there is a big difference in attitude about the changes that should be proposed. He proposes further restrictions. I, and I hope many of my colleagues, see it as being a time to give full consideration to broadening the kinds of facilities in which abortions can be performed. We should work with the provinces on that. As well, we should work to ultimately remove from the Criminal Code the issue of abortion to enable women to make that kind of choice themselves.
To come back to the point I made earlier, a one-hour debate in Private Members' Hour is not sufficient to hear all the views so sincerely held by my colleagues. I am sure that at some future time we will have the opportunity to express our
views on this most vital issue. I would like to thank my colleague for bringing this matter to the House today, but I do not propose to support his motion and I ask for the support of my colleagues for the position I have taken.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-226 introduced by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley). The right to life is one of the basic premises of our society and I share my hon. colleague's views, as 1 am sure all Hon. Members do, that protection for the unborn is of the utmost importance. This simple statement is of crucial significance, particularly to the abortion debate. It is becoming increasingly apparent that there is a significant decrease in concern for the sanctity of life around the world.
Respect for life has undergone a tragic change in recent years. It has gone from "sacred" status down to "important". In society today it is more and more widely held that life should be protected but only until some other "important" consideration comes along. The obvious examples of this today are the increasing popularity of concepts like euthanasia and abortion on demand. Some people today say it is all right to have an abortion if you have an important reason. This kind of excuse has been broadened to include the most trifling inconvenience. Obviously when people say life is sacred, they mean completely different things.
The point of this Bill, which I wholeheartedly support, is that most Canadians believe life is sacred. Unless this belief is reflected in legislation, we will be guilty of raising a generation which has no conception of lasting values. They will have been sacrified for expedience and convenience. Society's laws are always a reflection of the moral norms which anchor our society. The abortion rights' movement has reversed this relationship. By putting something into law they can restructure our values. By legalizing abortion on demand they can create a new morality for our society. Whenever society believes it can create its own morality, it is in trouble. The most obvious result of this self-reliance is irresponsibility to any sense of value altogether. History has shown us that rebellion, disorder and confusion inevitably follow. We must focus today on responsibility, not on rights.
This excellent piece of legislation will have the opposite effect. It will restore the legal framework of our society to a state consistent with the values which have formed the bedrock of not only our society but every society which comes to mind. This legislation confers respect on the most important moral law by giving meaning to the expression we all uphold, that of the sanctity of life. It seems ironic that in a day and age when we are spending billions of dollars to save lives through medical research, we are at the same time permitting the murder of thousands and thousands of unborn infants.
I would like to conclude by once again thanking the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake for sponsoring this excellent and timely piece of legislation. I hope Members of this House will take the opportunity they have to make this most significant improvement to our Criminal Code by giving their support for this Bill and allowing it to go to committee.
September 12, 1985

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in the adjournment debate and to consider more specifically a question I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) a while ago regarding the future of the automobile industry in Canada and Japanese car imports.
Mr. Speaker, the day I asked my question, there were a lot of developments. And I think the announcement made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) today is very reassuring. I would like to join all Members of this House in congratulating the Hyundai company, which not only has confidence in Canada but, from what the Minister told us, decided on its own to consider locating in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, at the present time the Lavalin group, for instance, is proceeding with studies to determine the best location for the company. I have a few suggestions to make.
I see the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand), and I am sure she will agree with me when 1 sing the praises of the City of Bromont which is located in her riding but provides jobs for both her riding and mine.
Mr. Speaker, you may know that demographically speaking, the City of Bromont has a population that is growing at a slightly faster rate than Quebec as a whole. The Bromont region, which, of course, includes Granby, Cowansville, and Waterloo, has great potential for Hyundai because it has a young population with more people under 25 and fewer people over 35, compared to the rest of Quebec. The population has a varied linguistic background, a large percentage of university graduates and a highly skilled labour force.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, as far as industrial considerations are concerned, Hyundai would do well to consider the City of Bromont, because the region has had the benefit of prudent and enterprising municipal authorities who, by creating industrial parks and promoting their availability, have
Adjournment Debate
been able to attract over 250 businesses and generate nearly 17,000 jobs in industry.
The area has a very diversified industrial makeup with industries representing most of the major sectors, with particular emphasis on high technology sectors. I do not think it is necessary to refer to them by name since Hon. Members know of them and they would only be jealous.
As far as recreation and quality of life are concerned, I am sure that future Hyundai employees will find happiness and tranquility in the Eastern Townships.
I am therefore pleased with today's announcement, Mr. Speaker, and I dare hope that our wishes will be fulfilled. 1 must say, however, that I am disappointed with the attitude of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion who washes his hands of the other matters just as he did of the Hyundai matter. A Toyota plant is coming and I know that the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) has put together a group to attract it and I support her in her efforts. I hope that she will tell the Parliamentary Secretary, among others, to intervene on behalf of the Eastern Townships, as we have some 12,000 unemployed who are on welfare and anxious to work for the Toyota firm, Mr. Speaker. We are also interested in a Suzuki plant. Of course, there is the Bombardier company who operates already in the city of Valcourt and which has made a name for itself in the building of jeeps, military trucks, and which was awarded a great many contracts under the Liberal Government. It has acquired much expertise and trained a pool of skilled workers and is itself eager to start one day a car manufacturing company of its own. Mr. Speaker, I do not claim that we will some day resemble the South-Western Ontario area, but I am convinced that if there is a political will and if the various authorities consider objectively-I repeat, objectively-the conditions which exist in the Eastern Townships, they will immediately realize that it would be the perfect site for such a plant.
Over the next few weeks and months, I think that we will make a point of keeping an eye on the situation as it develops, because the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion is not particularly keen on our region. As you know, we have had the Domtar experience, and if the past is any indication of the future, we know that we should not rely too much on him. I urge therefore my Quebec colleagues to be vigilant. This past Summer, I reminded some of them that it was their duty to work on the automobile plant issue and I see my friend the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) who woke up and precisely sought for his riding what I am seeking for mine, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I am almost tempted to say something about the great automobile City of Windsor and its super offer to Toyota. It would give magnificant possibilities to the many unemployed in my constituency. However, that is not the question before us this evening.
My question concerns Mitel. Of course it may seem a little out of date to be returning to a question which was raised on May 15. However, interestingly enough, the question is even more striking now than it was at the time. At that point the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) was asked whether he would meet urgently with Mitel management to urge them to accept an 18 per cent takeover bid from British Telecom instead of the 51 per cent takeover which they wished to accept.
If that 18 per cent had been accepted, this would have given Mitel the cash which it required to do what was necessary to restore its financial viability by reducing its debt load. The basic problem of Mitel is a very significant debt load which has to be paid off and is responsible for the significant losses which the company continues to experience.
Originally our problem with the suggested takeover was that British Telecom was far too much influenced by and subject to the pressures of British legislation and British Government ownership. Second, we felt that this helped to contribute to the likely shift of employment from here in Canada to the United Kingdom and third, that as a follow-through from this job loss, there was also the potential that research and development would shift from Canada to Britain as the ownership and control by British Telecom came into place. Frankly, we also
felt that Mitel was one of the important high-tech players in our economy and that it was important for our economic future for Government to support the role of high-tech industry.
Interestingly enough, the last two months of recess of the House have shown in dramatic fashion that the concerns we raised about Mitel were absolutely justified. We have seen that the Mitel takeover in Britain has been referred to the Monopolies Commission of that country. The Monopolies Commission in Britain has very significant powers. It has flexibility and a capacity to set conditions on takeovers, a capacity which is far beyond anything we have in the Canadian economy. While it is quite unlikely that the British Monopolies Commission will refuse to permit British Telecom to make any purchase of Mitel shares, it is quite likely that the Monopolies Commission will put in place severe conditions on the takeover.
Some of the conditions that are most likely to be put into effect come from the fact that the companies concerned in Britain are the potential competitors to Mitel for British Telecom business. They are particularly concerned that Mitel would be given preferential treatment as a supplier to British Telecom. That, incidentally, was the point used by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion to defend his support of the Mitel takeover.
It is quite likely that, because of the concern of these British companies, one of the conditions which the British Monopolies Commission will impose will be that Mitel will not be able to have a preferential position with respect to purchases made by British Telecom of telephone equipment. We are likely to lose that potential advantage. A likely additional condition that could be imposed by the British Monopolies Commission will be the authorization of a percentage of takeover lower than 51 per cent.
The second major development in the Mitel saga has been the recent announcement by the company that 440 jobs will be cut from its operations in Canada. Some of these jobs are in fact being shifted to other operations in Canada, but some are being transferred, as we predicted, to the U.K.
That brings me to a set of questions, Mr. Speaker. First, where was government leadership in trying to make Mitel a continuing high-tech leader in this country? Did the Government explore other private sector options? Dit it have discussions with Mitel to offer government help? Finally, why did the Government not take the advice we offered in May to have Mitel adopt an 18 per cent share offer from British Telecom which would have avoided the subsequent problems with the British Monopolies Commission, leaving Mitel and its employees very much hanging in limbo?
We have asked these questions. We hope the Government will finally give us some answers to them.
September 12, 1985
