speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the Hon. Member's request last May, the Minister did in fact meet with the President of Mitel to find out where the company was headed.
At the time, Mr. Matthews informed the Minister that British Telecom was seeking to acquire control over the company, following common practice by taking an unconditional option on the purchase of 18.5 per cent of Mitel common shares. This percentage constitutes the maximum allowed under the regulations of the stock exchange and is meant to protect British Telecom from speculation on Mitel shares, pending decisions by the shareholders, the regulatory agencies and the courts. If the proposal is not accepted, British Telecom will have to decide whether or not to lift its option. Since the option on 18.5 per cent of the shares is unconditional, Mitel management might not be able to influence British Telecom's decision. Investment by the latter in Mitel would inject $320 million of fresh equity into the company, which it urgently needs to finance future expansion.
Mitel has needs that are common among hi-tech companies, in that it requires rapid access to capital as the company develops. During the last two years, it was able to maintain a remarkable rate of growth in sales, but on the whole, its financial results have been meagre. This poor performance has closed the doors to the financial markets to which its competitors have access and has severely taxed the resources of management which had to find alternative solutions.
Mitel recently launched a new type of automatic switcher, the SX 2000, developed in this country by Canadians with federal assistance, which will be one of Mitel's main products in the future. It will not be offered on the traditional markets, and to ensure its success, the company must dispose of the funds required to set up new distribution channels. If as a result of Government regulation, Mitel is prevented from getting access to financial markets, there is a possibility that Canada will not enjoy any of the financial benefits.
Mitel has shown it is capable of developing and manufacturing, in Canada, products that can be sold on the international market. The international telecommunications market is highly regulated and protected, and the fact that Mitel was able to overcome these obstacles demonstrates its strong competitive position.
Canadian businesses must have access to the most sophisticated communications techniques available to remain competitive, and Canadians who design and produce this technology should not be discriminated against in their own country.
In its report entitled Telecommunications in Canada, Part III, The Impact of Vertical Integration on Equipment Industry, tabled on January 7, 1983, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission recommends that Bell be more receptive to inno-
Adjournment Debate
vations developed in Canada by businesses other than its own subsidiaries.
I would also like to come back to what the Hon. Member said about the transfer or loss of jobs at Mitel. The decision made by Mitel to transfer part of its production is an attempt to improve its operational effectiveness and profit-making position. For the last two years, this company has suffered losses. It has indicated that it is facing excess capacity. By transfering production and employees from Kanata to Renfrew, it would be in a better position to compete.
Estimates by the company itself clearly indicate that the number of jobs lost is, will be significantly lower than the one mentioned by the Hon. Member, and this decision will allow at least some Mitel employees to keep their jobs.

THE BUDGET-IMPACT ON AGRICULTURE. (B) EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 26 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) if he would be willing to consider giving an exemption to farmers from the two cents a litre, nine cents a gallon, excise tax which he imposed in his Budget of May 23. In his response he was very evasive. He suggested that in fact the price of gasoline was going down for farmers. That was highly prophetic because when he spoke in the House and ate his humble pie, due to the old age pension reversal of the Government two days later, he in fact added another cent per litre or four and a half cents a gallon.
The reason I asked that question, Mr. Speaker, was that in the election campaign a year ago the Government made a clear statement that second on their list of agricultural commitments was a reduction in the price of farm fuel by 20 cents a gallon by removing the nine cents a gallon federal sales tax and by not collecting the current excise tax. It is my understanding that the Government is still collecting that original excise tax although it is being refunded.
Last November in fact the Government removed the excise tax on gasoline and gave an exemption to the petroleum compensation charge. That amounted to 4.8 cents per litre of gasoline for primary producers. However, on the first of June the Government moved to world price for gasoline and the exemption for farmers of 1.8 cents per litre was, of course, cancelled. However, the price of gasoline did not go down so that exemption was not available. In fact, the price of gasoline to farmers went up by 1.8 cents a litre on June 1. On September 3 the Government increased the excise tax on gasoline by 2 cents a litre, 9 cents a gallon. If we add the two together, the increase in price on June 1 and September 3, the primary producers end up paying 3.8 cents per litre additional or some $130 million on an annualized basis.
The Government clearly made a committee in the election campaign that it would take away the excise tax and reduce the price of farm fuels. I would hope that the Parliamentary Secretary, a distinguished Member of Parliament who I know

September 12, 1985
Adjournment Debate
has the best interests of agriculture at heart, will want to come clean and indicate that the Government is prepared to keep its election campaign promises and will remove that excise tax. It clearly is unfair. It is being imposed at a time when western Canada, all parts of Canada, are facing severe stress in agricultural commodities, such as the prices for hogs, beef and grain. On top of that, there are drought conditions in the west which are absolutely devastating.
I mentioned earlier that the Minister of Finance was going to impose an additional cent per litre on January 1, 1987. Of course, the other three cents per litre runs out on December 31, 1986. So during the next 16 months, combined with the last three months, we will see an increase in fuel prices for farmers of at least 31 cents or 32 cents per gallon, which is totally and completely contrary to what was promised during the election campaign.
There is a very serious situation in agriculture today. Bankruptcies and foreclosures are rising dramatically. World commodity prices for beef, hogs, and grain are dropping. In view of this, I hope the Government will decide to keep its campaign promise and reduce the two cents per litre or nine cents per gallon excise tax on farm fuels which it imposed just last week.
Everything I have said applies, of course, to the forestry, fishing and mining industries. There was a campaign promise that the excise tax would be removed, yet the Budget indicated that the tax is going to go up at a time when fuel prices should be going down. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary is able to tell us that the Government is prepared to keep its promise and remove the excise tax.

The Government is very concerned about the immediate problem facing farmers as well as the longer term challenges facing this vitally important component of the Canadian economy.

We are fully aware, Mr. Speaker, of all the problems now facing farm producers. We have reduced the cost of gasoline and removed taxes. These measures will come into force on December 1st, 1985.

The Petroleum Fuel Tax rebate reduced the price of farm fuels by 21.6 cents per gallon. When added to the rebate of the excise tax the effective saving to farmers was 28 cents per gallon.

It must be kept in mind that all these efforts have been made during the year. We are going to do more. We have fulfilled almost all our election commitments, Mr. Speaker. My colleague from Algoma (Mr. Foster) knows this very well for he is monitoring activities in committee and in here. He is aware of our work, and it is my view that this Government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has met its obligations to Canadian farm producers, Mr. Speaker.
